She entrusts her with various tasks concerning the house and some Sisters.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Listen carefully to what you must do. You must send me — or rather bring yourself — the Lucera and Legnano contracts;1 have the small harmonium well crated2 and send it to Florence; tell Bruni to take care not to do as with the one sent to Ferrara, which was badly crated and completely ruined.

2. Do not send the teacher I told you to send to Florence after all; I have arranged everything. For pity's sake do not send novices anywhere, for — you will hear in person.3

3. For pity's sake handle Sr. A. Michelina well, for everything is being done for her health; if you think fit to accompany her, do so, but she will suffer at knowing you are coming here and she is not. When the Father arrives I will hear what he says and write to you again about it.4

4. Meanwhile write and tell me which Sisters are still lacking for Matera, or whether they are all there, for I have decided Sr. A. Prudenzina is unsuitable; if she fell ill it would make a very bad impression.

5. If you have any more, older ones are fine, but not novices, no.5 I hope some postulants have reached you; if you can send the 300 lire to the one who is tormenting you, see to it.6

I stop, as I must go out; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Of the two recently opened Houses.

2 Have the harmonium well packed.

3 ... you will hear in person. The S. Congregation had forbidden it.

4 Cf. L 490, n. 3.

5 ... older ones. She means not in age but in vocation.

6 A postulant who had returned to her family.

She advises and encourages the Superior, who with the Sisters assigned to start a new work at Rutigliano has had to stop in Bari with the Sisters of Charity.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I hear what you say about Sr. A. Clarenza's diploma, but what am I to do? You can tell them you thought they meant your pharmacist's diploma, and you must give them that at once;2 keep your spirits up, for the saint will help you in everything.

2. Certainly it would have been better for you to wait at the Sisters' house; don't worry at all whether they will be paid; you will certainly be a trouble to them.3

Be sure to edify, but don't worry, there is no harm.

3. Courage, understood? Never get upset. Greetings to all the sisters.

4. As for the diploma, you can tell them I will send it later; I did not think it was needed, as they had not mentioned it.

Goodbye; the Lord bless you; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 By an evident slip the L was filed among those of November instead

of December, as the historical context shows. Cf. Index IV, 23.

2 To the school authorities asking for Sr. A. Clarenza

Devoto's qualification the Superior had replied that she would hand it over. In fact she did not

have it.

3 After a few days in Bari the Superior had gone to Ru

tigliano to hasten the completion of their lodgings.

She specifies the day of departure. Instructions and tasks.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. I have your long letter with Sr. A. Stimatina's enclosed. I hope you received my last. Now that I have spoken with the Father, you will leave with Michelina on the 19th or 20th of this month; so you will be here and we will spend holy Christmas together.

2. Lock up well and leave nothing out; give strict orders to Sr. A. Grazia — woe to her if she gives anything away; tell Sr. A. Angelica to be good, and then she shall have everything and I will bring her something nice.2

3. As for postulants, none can be accepted for now unless they have [£] 1000; so those already accepted, yes, but no new ones.3 Have Sr. A. Dafrosa make her will, and Sr. A. Gabriella too would be wise; tell her it is for the Lodi house, which is in her name; the Bishop wants it.4

4. For the sister you may write to Lodi. For pity's sake let her do well and not fall ill; find out whether she is healthy.5 I am sending you a letter; reply to Sr. A. D. tomorrow.6 Those for Chiaravalle leave tomorrow.

5. Tell Sr. A. Gabriella to go and see the workmen, and if it freezes so that they cannot work, she must make them stop; let her keep an eye on it.7 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 These two Sisters had responsible roles in the general services of the

Mother House.

3 Cf. L 490,5-6.

4 The will was required by Canon Law. Here it was urgent

and necessary, since the Sisters held title to some of the Institute's properties (as

it was a body not recognised by the State) and had to name other Sisters

as heirs, so that on their death the property would not pass by

law to their relatives.

5 She was to write to Sr. A. Sapienzina at Lodi, telling her of the

Mother's wish that she go to Matera.

6 There is no information to identify the Sister.

7 The workmen were building a wing of the house.

Cf. L 500,2.

She encloses a letter for Don Francesco Chemin, which she is to read to him in person. The alms-collectors are about to return. She should be cheerful.

A.M.F.

Dear daughter,

1. Be careful he does not snatch it from your hands; be strong, and God will reward you greatly.2

2. I send you 50 F. The alms-collectors have gone back to collecting in Verona, for they had done very little and visited only a few houses. Now most of the work lies ahead.

3. Cheer up, for they will bring you plenty; but give nothing to that wretch, nothing; he must already have taken more than 3000 F.3

What a business! What do you say? I assure you it greatly upsets me. Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. Genoveffa's reply: 13.12.'81.

2 Be careful... greatly. In the L mentioned above Sr. A. Genoveffa told the

Mother she had read her letter to Don Francesco with difficulty, in obedience,

praying in her heart that the Lord would "raise up the house" and inter

vene with his mighty help to free it from the tangle of interests weighing on everyone.

3 Cf. L 497.

She sends offerings for Masses to be said.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Here you are. By return of post, a few Masses, though I really have very few now.1 Have people pray for me. As for the alms-collector, do as you think best;2 in haste,

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 421.

2 She had replaced one of the alms-collectors.

Encouragement. She tells her the lawyer is coming to settle the matter and awaits news.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Courage, for it is a time of trials, but Jesus is with us. Cheer up!

2. As soon as I received your letter2 I telegraphed the lawyer to go there with Don Francesco's receipts;3 be at peace, everything will be settled. I long for you to write me something; I really want to know. I was expecting Sr. A. Corinna today; I hope she will come tomorrow. I truly want to know how far that wretch has gone!

3. I learn from the letter just received. How dreadful; I am telegraphing with reply paid. My God, what deeds of the wretch he is!4

4. May God give you strength to bear everything with resignation. For pity's sake don't let it upset you; be at peace, for Jesus is with you and I am close to you and do not leave you for a minute. What deeds! How cleverly he managed the business!5

5. As for the postulant, she cannot be accepted — I will tell you in person or write another time — unless they have £ 1000. So you see?6 Courage, daughter, for pity's sake; yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 Dated 12.12.'81.

3 The lawyer Alberto Galli went to Bassano to clarify the matter of Don

Francesco Chemin and his family. Cf. his report to M. Rosa: 20.12.'81, AFSA,

Foundations.

4 On 13.12.'81 the Superior had told M. Rosa, among other things, that Don

Francesco had intercepted the Sisters' letters.

5 What deeds! The Chemin sisters claimed "all Don

Francesco's things, and all the church things". He had also listed "many things

not his own". Cf. L 441, n. 2; 450,4.

6 ... unless they have £ 1000. Such was the order of the S. Congregation of Bishops and

Regulars. Cf. L 490,5.

She allows her to go to Bologna for some purchases and encourages her to love poverty and uprightness.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. What you write about the poor little nuns, alas, is true; as I have no time to dwell on it,1 I pass quickly on to allowing you to go to Bologna to buy what you need.2 Courage, for whoever is poor is sure to be dear to Jesus. As for the eggs and onions, the Father says that if everyone was taking them, you could take some too.3 Goodbye,

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 To carry out the law suppressing the monasteries, "the government

forces" entered the Capuchin nuns' monastery and made the nuns

leave. Sr. A. Agnese went to help the poor things carry away their belongings.

Reporting to the Mother on 14.12.'81 she did not hide her surprise at the great

quantity of goods and provisions in the convent, and expressed it to M. Rosa with a judgement,

asking whether what had happened was a trial or a punishment from the Lord. The Mother

refrains from comment, having no time to dwell on it. But she draws one certainty: whoever is

poor is sure to be dear to Jesus.

2 She allows her to go to Bologna. She was to buy spectacles for a

Sister and other necessities.

3 In the turmoil of the expulsion the helpers took something

of what the nuns left behind. Sr. A. Agnese had scruples about having taken

"some eggs and about ten onions". Fr Tornatore reassures her.

Advice for her and for the Superior of the "Ardizzone" Institute.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have yours with the receipt, thank you;1 and now in haste I tell you not to write to Sr. A. Clemente, for Z resents it... you understand?2

2. So tell Sr. A. Clemente to manage on her own and to insist that they pay her salary; let her press hard; I forgot to write it to her. Thanks to your prayers the Father is much better.3

Your affectionate M. ROSA

1 The receipt for sending the fruit basket. Cf. L 489,1.

2 To avoid upsetting the directors of the "Ardizzone" Institute, the Superior Crocifissa

preferred to send the Superior Clemente Bigatti by letter the advice she thought

useful, rather than visit her in person. But this displeased Canon Ignazio

Zuccaro.

3 Cf. L 485,2; 489,2.

She is to send off a Sister and ask the master builder for his bill. Other tasks.

A.M.E

My daughter,

1. You tell me about Sr. A. Incoronata; I would send her for a while to Sr. A. Camilla and commend her, explaining her character very clearly.1 Tell her this in my name.

2. Tell the master builder to send me his full bill for this year, so that the count can check it and the money be sent. Pay Ratti, who has written to me, and Fiorugi, and the meat bill.

3. Listen, please send some sheets, 6 pillowcases, 10 towels and some kitchen linen; send them all dirty, for they will have them washed at Sestri. Tell them so — dirty sheets too, as long as they are good. Goodbye; the carriage is here and I must go out,2

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 As the Superior Francesca was to go to Rome, it was not wise

to leave this Sister at the Mother House. The Mother suggests entrusting her to Sr. A.

Camilla Valentini, Superior at the hospital of Borgo S. Donnino.

2 The carriage is here; I must go out.

She introduces a gentleman and asks her to receive him and treat him with every attention and courtesy.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A gentleman will come to you with a note from me; receive him well; you see, he is Commendatore Dulsaque of the tobacco factory.1

2. He would like you to be like a sister to him. I mean, when he is well settled at home, he would like you to see to his linen and ironing; in short, I want you to be ready to do all you can to serve him. In short, receive him well.

3. I don't know how to put it; I want him to be satisfied; make him a thousand offers of service2 and you will see you will be glad of it; always with your companion.3

4. Show him the house; see that it is in good order, with no bad smells, and the girls in white aprons; cleanliness, in short; it will do you much good; I urge it warmly. Greet him for me and give him my regards; I am

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 One of the administrators of the "Incunabolo" for the children of the women working at the

Tobacco Factory in Rome. Cf. Index IV, 14.

2 ... a thousand offers: always showing herself ready to serve him.

3 Always with your companion: the Rule forbade ever dealing

alone with "persons of the other sex".

Exhortation and advice. She cannot allow vows to be taken in December.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. God continues to give you his light; and you, my dear, try courageously to act on it.

2. As for the gardener, I leave you entirely free to do what you think best; I will approve everything.1

3. As for vows, they cannot be allowed, for we take them on Saint Anne's day; so she will take them then.2 For the rest, try to find out as much as you can.3 So courage; pray for me and believe me

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 As for the gardener... The Superior, considering that the Mother had to make

"Sacrifices to pay the house's debts", proposed, to help her finan

cially, to run the livestock themselves instead of the farmer. Cf. L to

M. Rosa: 19.12.'81.

2 The Superior, on behalf of Sr. A. Melania, asked permission for her to take vows.

3 To "find out" Don Francesco's interference and manoeuvres in the administration

of the Institute. The Superior had learned of one of Don

Francesco's "operations". In the previous Superior's time he had sold a piano

worth Fr. 700, a gift to the Sisters, for Fr. 400. The buyer

immediately resold it for 760 Fr. This was only one of many.

Christmas greetings and expressions of gratitude.

Most Reverend Excellency,

1. With the liveliest eagerness I fulfil the sacred duty I owe you, Most Reverend Father, by offering you on this happy feast of Holy Christmas my most fervent good wishes, together with those of the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, for the preservation of your precious days. Yes, may the Holy Child prolong them far into the future, fill you with his graces and make you happy in this lowly exile, among the blessed, and grant you a good end and a better beginning of the year.

2. Accept these words as a token of my gratitude for all the good you do the poor Daughters of Saint Anne, and be assured that I pray the Lord may fill you with his graces.

3. Kindly, Most Reverend Father, offer a prayer for me at the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, that good Jesus may assist me with his grace.

Renewing my profound respects, I remain your

most devoted servant Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

She reassures her: she is pleased with her.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Be calm and at peace, for the letter I sent you was a mistake; it was meant for a sister who is not you.1 So cheer up, for I have nothing against you; carry on as you are doing,2 and Jesus will bless you.

2. Have a happy holy season; may the Child Jesus bless you all,

affectionate M. ROSA

1 A letter of reproof had been delivered to the Sister by mistake. The

Mother reassures her.

2 Sr. A. Giorgia was docile and full of good will.

She thanks her for what she sent and hopes the school year can be finished well.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Thank you for the capons; they arrived in excellent condition and at just the right time.1 God bless you.

2. If the sister is no use to you, I will tell you to send her.2 I hope you received another letter from me, though not in my own hand.

3. Signora Rusconi3 does not write to me and would like a qualified teacher, but she says so coolly. Let us hope we can get through the year without sending one.4

Goodbye. Be patient, I am in such a hurry. Yours for all ages,

affectionate M. ROSA

1 She had sent 12 capons for Christmas.

2 A novice recently arrived in the community was no help to her, wrote

Sr. A. Agnese. The Mother is willing to move her elsewhere.

1 Rusconi: the benefactress who promoted the parish school in collaboration with the Sisters.

4 Let us hope we can finish the school year without sending the qualified teacher.

Advice on the house's financial problem and the Chemin affair.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. How glad I am that the alms-collectors have gathered so much!1

2. Listen, pay no debts at all, understood? None, neither small nor large. Remember that on the first of February [£] 1256 fall due, a mistake made by our lawyer.2 We are not to pay debts.

3. Likewise the chalice: if you have none I will send you one, for I have a spare.3 Spend nothing on the house, for it is not wise. You will hear later.

4. Try to find out exactly how much money Chemin has received, for pity's sake.4 The Superiors want to see the contract and I can never get hold of it; what a trial!

5. I am unwell; pray and have others pray for me, for I really do not know how to react. Goodbye,

affectionate M. ROSA

1 Coming home from Venice they brought Fr. 454, according to the Superior Genoveffa

Molinari.

2 Listen... lawyer. She refers to the debts burdening Don Francesco and the

financial situation in which the Institute is involved. Cf. L 497,1.

3 The chalice had been seized along with other objects. Cf. Index IV, 10.

4 Cf. L 502, n. 3.

The accounts are in order. She asks for news of the sick and the alms-collectors.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have your letter with the accounts; all is well. You tell me nothing about the sick1 or the alms-collectors.2 Did you know two Capuchin alms-collectors raised six thousand lire in Milan? Oh! if only that happened to you, what good fortune! Please God! Have people pray for me and believe me yours for ever,

affectionate M. ROSA

1 Cf. L 466, n. 4.

2 Cf. L 470, n. 2.

8. CARACCIOLO (Count) FRANCESCO. Born in Piacen za on 7.6.1811, he died there on 26.11.1896. Throughout his life he used his considerable income in charity for the poor. With his brother Maurizio he founded the Society of St Vincent de Paul in Piacenza and was long its president. He took up painting and produced several works, and earned merit by his intelligent patronage of needy young artists. After the deaths of his sister Isabella in 1880 and his brother in 1889, he gave the family properties to charity. He greatly helped the religious and public institutions of Piacenza, above all the Daughters of Saint Anne, to whom, on the advice of his great friend Fr G. B. Tornatore, he left the large Gargatano estate. He also held Mother Rosa in high esteem; she was in contact with the Caracciolo family. L 96; 125; 129.

III. INDEX OF NOTABLE PERSONS NAMED IN THE CORRESPONDENCE

1. ACCINELLI (Canon) ANTONIO. For general and particular

information on his relations with Mother Rosa and

with the Institute, see Index III of the volumes: Letters 3, pp.

741-42; Letters 4, p. 652; Letters 5, p. 666.

Don Accinelli's 16 letters of 1880 to the Mother clearly show his friendship for her, his love for the Institute and the zeal with which he took to heart the smooth running of the houses at Genoa, Sampierdarena and Sestri. With a frankness that was often blunt he put delicate and difficult situations before the Mother, suggesting solutions or asking her to intervene. His requests for Sisters to meet the many calls for home nursing, or for the transfer of others who were unsuitable or ill, were weighed and taken into account by the Mother. His competence made him a great help in financial matters, as in any administrative or legal matter in dealings with civil and religious authorities.

There remained, however, a basic problem: the difficulty of getting on with the Superior of the Genoa house, and this was what led him to renounce (L to M.R. 24.10.1880) all responsibility for and interest in the Institute. AFSA B.4.95.

In this volume the Mother mentions him in letters to various Sisters: L 89, n. 1; 133, n. 3; 142, n. 1; 218,7 and n. 7; 224, 2 and notes 4-6.

2. CUSTO ALESSANDRO. In M. Rosa

Gattorno's correspondence published so far (vols. 1-5) there are the following references to her son

Alessandro Custo: Letters 1, p. 521; Letters 4,

p. 642; Letters 5, pp. 666-67.

Mother Rosa's letters to her son from 1880-81 are lost, but his letters to her survive: seven from 1880, five from 1881. Alessandro was not causing her great sorrow; he had married and was trying to set up his own business, so the Mother rarely mentions him to the Sisters who knew and had helped him. To Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni (L 124,11) she writes: "He has really settled down well, has taken a wife and has a son. He has set up a fine, very large lime works. I hope everything from God, that he may bless him and

help him do everything well. You pray too". She passes on his greetings from Piacenza, where he had come on a visit with his wife, to Sr. A. Benedetta, who was taking the baths at Sestri (L 180,1). Another time, from Rome, she tells Carlotta and Gaspare about a two-day visit and remarks on the habits of her daughter-in-law and grandson (L 291,2).

Letters in which the Mother mentions her son: L 124,10-11; 180,1, n. 1; 262, n. 11; 291,2, n. 1; 306,1, n. 1; 308,3, n. 3; 344, n. 1-2.

3. TORNATORE (Father) GIOVANNI BATTISTA. The Father is present in the life of the Institute through the by now indispensable service he felt called to render alongside Mother Rosa, both internally as the Foundress's adviser and externally in legal and administrative matters connected with the Institute's life and growth; hence in four of the five volumes published so far (cf. Letters 5, p. 664) he appears in Index III among the "notable persons" who corresponded with the Foundress but whose letters from her have not survived. In Letters 5, however, he appears among the addressees, since that volume publishes as no. 232 one of the two letters of Mother Rosa to the Father found among "the papers of the Barbiellini family", dated but without addressee, yet certainly attributable to him. The second, of 1884 (cf. AFSA A 1.10. Mald '84), will be published in due course.

In this volume of the correspondence Mother Rosa and her correspondents often refer to Fr Tornatore, and these references, brief and often mere allusions, reveal a deep reality emerging in the fabric of daily life through the events and people of our history. Among those people the figure of the Father stands out with homely simplicity and authority.

Many of the Sisters who knew him and experienced his fatherly wisdom and enlightened counsel asked the Mother in their letters to beg the Father to pray for them, or to greet him; and the Mother in turn passed on his "remembrance" to her distant daughters. Two examples: to Sr. A. Giuseppa Troni: ... "the Father, with Sr. A. Benedetta, Alessandro and Carlotta, send greetings" (L 115); to Sr. A. Francesca Savignone: "The Father sends greetings and thanks you for your letter" (L 47). When the Father was ill the Mother concerned herself with his health and, if away from Piacenza, asked for news (L 52), informed the Sisters of the other Houses and asked them to pray. "They wri-

te from Piacenza that the Father is very ill; have people pray" (L 486; 489; 499). When, having recovered in December 1881, he was about to leave for Rome with Carlotta and her family, the Mother hastened to warn the Superior of the Florence house of their stop there, with particular solicitude: "I commend to you the children and the poor Father" (L 488).

The Father's name day, 24 June, was one occasion for honouring him. "Today we are celebrating here, as you surely are there too", she wrote to Sr. A. Francesca Savignone, who had sent a pandolce from Genoa for the occasion (L 396). The Mother would not tolerate careless omission of the marks of respect then customary towards the Father, especially at particular moments. "Tell the novice mistress — she writes to the Superior of Piacenza — that when they arrived not one greeted the Father, who was present; instead of kneeling and asking his blessing, nothing. Ask her whether this is the training she gives them, and what she teaches them. What a pity!" (L 65).

Fr Tornatore's presence in the House of the Saint — as he used to call it — was a source of security for Mother Rosa, especially when she was away visiting other houses, for Sr. A. Francesca Savignone, the young Superior, would ask him what to do, particularly in urgent cases, while waiting for the Mother's instructions or reassurance: "All the Father has had you do is right" (L 281). The Mother herself relied on his judgement, consulting him before taking important decisions or answering particular questions from the Superiors: "When the Father comes I will hear what he says" (L 490; 492); "As for the kitchen, that is fine; do as you say; I spoke to the Father and he said it can be done that way" (L 448); "the Father says you could do it" (L 498).

Fr Tornatore's work is also evident beyond the Mother House, in the Institute's general activities: the opening of new houses and related problems (L 256), and relations with civil and religious figures (L 369; 376; 377; 379; 453). On more than one occasion the Mother asked him to accompany her on visits to the Houses. In the two years under review, according to the brief and incomplete indications of the correspondence, in 1880 the Father was at Pistoia (L 76), Rome (L 76), Naples (L 102; 115), and again Rome (L 124). The following year he joined the Mother in Rome in January (L 290; 294) and again in December (L 488; 490; 492; 498; 499).

Circular letters signed by M. Rosa and Fr Tornatore: L 24; 267.

IV. THE FOUNDATIONS (1880-1881)

The Houses are listed in chronological order of opening.

1. LODI (MI). Orphanage

The "House of Providence", which sheltered 35 poor girls, had been running for seven years under the Sisters of "St Mary Magdalene" of Turin when, on 24 October 1879, they proposed to the Mother Foundress of the Daughters of Saint Anne that she take over the work, which suited her Institute's purpose, while they were obliged to give it up as it did not fit their charism. They were handing over "the house they owned with all its furniture, clothing, linen, etc.". Mother Rosa was favourable and sought the approval of Bishop Domenico Gelmini, setting out her conditions: "Let the house be ceded to us in the form of a sale to two of our Sisters, with all that belongs to the orphanage. Let the entire administration and all that serves the full upkeep of the girls be ceded to us" (Letters 5, L 421). He agreed, with the conditions and aims he required: the establishment was to "remain always for the benefit of the city and diocese of Lodi through the Congregation of the Daughters of Saint Anne... to shelter abandoned, endangered and wayward girls, always dependent on the Bishop pro tempore" (L 2.3.1880 to M. Rosa Gattorno).

The Mother therefore set about organising the new work in its administrative and legal aspects. She appointed Sr. A. Genoveffa Molinari Superior; she reached Lodi on 2 January 1880 with two Sisters, Sr. A. Teresa Manzetti and Silvestra Pallotti, to take over the orphanage from the last of the former Sisters remaining there.

The first impact was hard. The Superior's dismay shows in her first report and later letters: "the house is poor, not to say very poor..."; everything had been taken away, even the blankets for the beds, and she had to borrow some and appeal to people's charity for offerings to feed the girls, some of whom received

a varying subsidy from the Charity Congregation of Lodi or Milan or other bodies and individuals — a subsidy which, moreover, not all of them paid. Alms-collecting therefore remained one of the sources of providence.

The Mother gradually sent more Sisters to cover all the duties: teaching and caring for the girls, general domestic services, home nursing, teaching catechism in some church, alms-collecting. With the Bishop's prior consent she also set aside part of the house as an infirmary for some sick sisters.

Finally she went there herself on 24.2.1880, before leaving for Rome, to see for herself and complete the general arrangements of the institute, and thought it best to entrust it to Sr. A. Costanza Cenni, granting Sr. A. Genoveffa's repeated wish.

The Lodi house, owned by the Congregation, with a large community engaged in important social services, was closely followed by her through her letters to the Superior (cf. the 26 letters to her in this volume) and to other Sisters of the community.

The people of Lodi appreciated and esteemed the "Annine" for their dedication and simplicity. In time the number of orphans grew and the quality of their education improved.

In 1889 an elementary day school was added, and later the premises were enlarged to meet the demands and needs of the times. Thus a boarding school and a hostel for students and working women came into being.

Over time the Institute has kept to its original purpose: caring above all for girls in special need. It now houses the "Stefano and Angela Danielli Residential Centre for the disabled", the hostel for young working women, the "First Reception Centre" for young women in difficulty, and the "Unitre" University for the elderly.

Cf. AFSA, Reg. Prot. 1876-1881, Nos. 372, 379, 500, 616. Foundations, Lodi. D.3.22.

2. PISA. Home nursing

Arrangements to entrust home nursing to the FSA were begun informally between Mgr Bar-

tolomeo Biscione, parish priest of San Michele in Borgo, Pisa, and the Superior of the Pistoia house, Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, who hastened to report to the Mother his goodwill towards the Sisters and his concrete proposals.

After visiting him while passing through Pisa, the Superior wrote to the Mother on 27 October 1879 that the parish priest would approach her as soon as he had something ready, concluding: "I am convinced much good can be done by opening the house in Pisa". Those directly concerned agreed that the Sisters would arrive by the end of January (L 8), but the Mother, unable to go herself, promptly commissioned the Superior Sr. A. Crocifissa, giving her precise instructions on 2 February (L 25). She arrived with Sr. A. Ancilla Briccoli, the future Superior of the new house, on 4 February 1880, as promised to the parish priest. The others — Sr. A. Taddea Accorsi, Bianca Bronchi, Cipriana Lapisè — arrived on the 20th, and two days later began nursing a French lady at home. To Sr. A. Crocifissa's precise and detailed reports the Mother responded with timely decisions: she would send more Sisters to meet the many requests for nursing and would replace the Superior (L 30, 34, 42). Finally she went herself on 14 March '80 (L 51). She was pleased and grateful for what the benefactors and Sisters had organised, and after a few days left them with the new Superior, Sr. A. Antonietta Gallinari, promising the help and support, when needed, of the Pistoia Superior Sr. A. Crocifissa, who by now knew the people, places and situation. This in fact happened (L 93, 100, 103, 107). She herself continued to encourage both, and left Pisa hoping they would do well. The Committee formed to support their work had provided not only a small furnished flat but also £ 1600 in monthly instalments for one year. Providence would do the rest — and providence did not fail the poor FSA or the sick. The reports first of Superior Antonietta and then of her successor Sr. A. Berarda Cattani stressed the community's good points: peace, observance, fidelity to the rule, and faithful fulfilment of its specific task, nursing the sick. When the Mother returned to Pisa in early December 1881 there were 9 Sisters; at least two more were needed, and they also had to move house for reasons of hygiene and ca-

pacity. The problem had to be solved. After consulting some Committee members, the Mother decided to have a more suitable dwelling found. Several people, among them some priests, hearing of the deserving nursing sisters' difficulty, gladly offered to help them and to extend their work to teaching. The best opportunity came from Count Curzio Desiderii, who gave the Sisters one of his houses with a small garden in Via S. Lorenzo, Pisa, rent-free for three years from July 1882.

A further improvement came with the purchase of a building in Via S. Maria, in the city centre. The "Saint Anne nurses" — as the people of Pisa called them — became a real institution in the city. In time, besides home nursing, the Sisters made themselves available for other social needs, taking into their house "both young and old", as the Prior of the Maddalena, Fr Jacopo Parrà, wrote on 25.10.1939 to the Superior General Sr. A. Corredentrice Pomarici. Hospitality prevailed with the opening of a university hostel, which continued, receiving on average 30 young people a year, until 1982, when the community had to be withdrawn for lack of religious personnel.

Cf. AFSA Reg. Prot. 1876-'81, Nos. 553, 554, 562, 566, 567. Superiors' correspondence with M. Rosa: F.5.41; D.3.24; D.4.31. Foundations, Pisa.

3. GIUGLIANO DI CAMPANIA (NA). Hospital

Negotiations between Mother Rosa and the Hospital Director, Fr Giuseppe Marzano, were soon concluded: from the request for three Sisters on 16.12.1879 to the sending of their travel money on 17.1.1880. When they reached Naples the Director was informed and came to meet them; they arrived on 7 February 1880, as the letter of the Superior Battistina Bertuzzi to the Mother shows. With her were Sr. A. Teodorica Sabini and Adalgisa Terroni.

In the hospital they found "a horror of filth... everything in disorder", writes the Superior, but soon everything was running regularly, orderly and clean.

The Mother visited on 13 April and stayed three days, to the great satisfaction of the Administration, from the Ma-

yor, President of the Hospital, to the Director and the people. They put to her directly the plan of entrusting the "Conservatorio" to her daughters.

The patients, on average 19-20, reached 60 in times of epidemic. The work increased, but everything went on in order as usual. "The Sisters are well, a little tired," wrote Sr. A. Battistina on 28.8.1880, "but there is the comfort of working gladly".

In 1901 the President of the "Charity Congregation" asked the then Superior General, Mother Benedetta Carrega, to assign the hospital a fourth Sister qualified in pharmacy, a request repeated in 1909; as none had the specific qualification, one was employed as an assistant.

In 1943, an "Old People's Poorhouse" having been added to the hospital, an Agreement was made between the "Municipal Welfare Board" and the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, obliging the Superior General to assign 8 Sisters to the Giugliano civil hospital, one as Superior in general charge and another as pharmacy assistant. The agreement was renewed at the set intervals. But in 1957, before the renewal, the President made it an indispensable condition that the number of Sisters be reduced "from 8 to 6", three of whom were to "be young and qualified as nurses". The Institute then considered withdrawing. For ten years painful negotiations went on, until the community was withdrawn from the hospital-home for lack of personnel in July 1968.

AFSA, Reg. Prot. 1876-'81, Nos. 532, 544, 548. Foundations, Giugliano di Campania. F.5.39. Letters of M. Rosa in this vol.: 90, 92, 96.

4. ARENA PO (PV). Hospital

Following agreements between the Administration of the S. Giacomo di Galizia hospital at Arena Po and Mother Rosa Gattorno as Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne, on 8 February 1880 in Piacenza the parties — the President Felice Pandini and Mother Gattorno — signed a renewable three-year agreement setting out the terms and obligations regarding the three Sisters

"charged with the internal, financial and disciplinary management of the Pious Institute".

On the following 15 February (L Savignone to M. Rosa 30.4.'80) Sr. A. Berta Belliti, Superior, arrived with Sisters Reparata Fabrini and Isabella.

The hospital, with some fifteen patients on average, was not in the best condition: there is "great disorder and filth," the Superior wrote to the Mother on 28.2.1880; "we are very well and pleased with the people of this town... we, and the Mayor too, want to have the Blessed Sacrament in the house as soon as possible, and a picture of Saint Anne", that is, a little chapel. The wish was granted a few months later.

From 1896 an FSA of the hospital community ran the nursery school in premises next to the hospital.

The Sisters were withdrawn from both works on 19 August 1960 for lack of personnel.

Cf. AFSA, Foundations, Arena Po. D.3,21.

5. PALERMO. Nurses' House - Provincial House (from 1884)

This was the first house opened in Palermo and the first in Sicily for home nursing. Until then the FSA had been in educational and welfare institutions: at Agrigento (1878), Termini Imerese (1878), Aci S. Antonio (1878) and Aci Catena (1878), with other requests awaiting a response. But Mother Rosa also had her "dear" sick at heart. She mentioned this wish to Canon Ignazio Zuccaro, who had visited her in Piacenza in September '79 and invited her to Palermo. She replied that she would come when a house for nurses had been set up there too, as in other cities.

Canon Zuccaro had brought with him to Piacenza Fr Domenico Bova, a friend he had encouraged to help the FSA with "something concrete", and together they undertook to fulfil the Foundress's wish.

He wrote to her on 7.10.1879 that his friend had worked, successfully, "to put your wish into practice" and had found room for the six nursing Sisters on the first floor of the small convent of San Marco. It was rather cramped, barely enough for 6 Sisters. But the

Superior of Termini, Sr. A. Gaudenzia Martinelli, had said the FSA were content with little, and the Archbishop himself, having seen the place, raised no objection in view of the Superior's opinion. Further details emerge from the later correspondence.

Fr Bova was willing to provide "the furnishings (what was needed) for the house, and the upkeep of the six Sisters for a year, trusting her (the Mother's) word that the Sisters would then make their own way" (5.2.1880). So little more than a month later (13.3.'80) Canon Zuccaro wrote: "everything is done... soon nothing will be lacking to receive the longed-for Daughters of Saint Anne... I wanted to oversee everything myself to do the best possible, since the excellent Fr Bova does not want to appear at all".

The Sisters arrived on 4 May 1880: Superior Sr. A. Del Salvatore Orsi, Sr. A. Macrina Paolini, Sr. A. Primitiva Boresi and Sr. A. Paolina Viani, joined by Sr. A. Sempliciana Saviotti of the Termini Imerese community, who had come to Palermo for dental treatment and stayed a few days. That same day the Superior reported to the Mother on the journey and their welcome. They had been "very warmly and courteously received by Vincenzina, sister of Fr Giacomo Cusmano", who had set up his "House of the Poor" in the same "little convent"; there the "Servants of the Poor" were being prepared — the Congregation actually born on 23 May 1880 with the clothing of the first six Sisters (L Sr. A. del Salvatore to M. Rosa). To make room for the FSA he had moved with the Brothers assisting him to other premises. (Cf. M. T. Falzone, below).

Fr Bova, writes the Superior in the same letter, had visited them, and as Canon Zuccaro was away from Palermo on visitation with Archbishop Celesia, he looked after them punctually and with a thousand attentions. He handed over the monthly allowance (£ 250), the travel money and whatever else was needed. On 8 May they began their service, nursing Princess Belmonte's maid. Sr. A. del Salvatore kept the Mother informed of the work's progress in frequent letters.

They all went together to visit the Archbishop. He encouraged them, foreseeing a harvest of good, and to open the way of charity to these "daughters of his" and make them known to the people of Palermo he had a circular letter published and distributed to the parish priests to be read to the faithful. The Superior's letters often mention the Archbishop: "he is keen for the Institute to spread"... "he came to visit unannounced"... "he is pleased with the Sisters,

he calls them affectionately 'my daughters'"... "he wants the Institute to go forward".

The number of patients grew, help was needed and M. Rosa sent more Sisters. Meanwhile the FSA became known elsewhere too, and requests came from Palermo, Mazara del Vallo, etc. Postulants also increased. A large house was now urgently needed. The Mayor was approached through Princess Emilia di Fitalia, and the Archbishop for his part charged his secretary Canon Zuccaro and Don Bova with the matter. After various searches and possibilities a solution was found: Mgr Gaetano Briuccia put a floor of his palace at Via dei Centurinai 48, Palermo, at the FSA's disposal, and they moved there at the end of February 1882 (L Orsi to M. Rosa: 25.2.'82).

In May 1884 the Sicilian communities were formed into a Province, and Sr. A. del Salvatore, while remaining Superior of the community, officially took on the role she was already filling in the other houses. She spared no effort and became a point of reference in Palermo and other cities. "Casa Briuccia" — as the Sisters called it — became the "Central" or Provincial House. The Spiritual Exercises were held there, and there the postulants stayed who in growing numbers sought to enter the FSA.

Sr. A. del Salvatore died prematurely on 7 June 1885 and was succeeded by Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, then Superior of the FSA community at the "S. Saverio" hospital in Palermo.

The nursing Sisters continued home nursing. They distinguished themselves by their utter dedication during the cholera of 1885, joined by many other Sisters sent by the Mother Foundress, "present and active everywhere, in the lazarettos, soup kitchens, wherever there was need, earning praise and admiration" (cf. M. T. Falsone in note).

In 1907 there was another move, because Mgr Briuccia's heirs asked the FSA to return the premises in exchange for farmland. They therefore moved into the building given to the FSA in 1896 by the Marquises Lancia di Brolo in Piazza S. Nicolò all'Albergheria. The Provincial Battistina Bertuzzi died on 17 February 1913. The valuable home-nursing service continued. On 18.2.1923 the Provincial Superior Sr. A. Getsemani Cornioli wrote to the then Mother General Sr. A. Camilla Valentini: "...there are many Sisters here, but nearly all are infirm; only six can work, and they must go out nursing by night and by

day, keep the house clean and help in the kitchen and chapel". These words show that home nursing was decreasing, partly because the Sisters had been engaged to work in hospitals, with specific duties laid down in agreements between the Superior General and the Administrations.

As for the Provincial House, in 1928 it was moved to the "Villa delle Rose" in Via Calatafimi.

Letters in this vol.: L 97, n. 4; 100, n. 2; 107,2; 115,5. M. Rosa's letters to Sr. A. del Salvatore have not survived.

Cf. AFSA, Prot. 1876-1881 nos. 349, 559, 573. Letters of Card. Celesia and Mgr Zuccaro: G.1.5. Letters of Sr. A. Salvatore Orsi. Foundations, Palermo - Lancia di Brolo. Letters of Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi: F.4.39-40. Sisters' letters: D.3.26; D.4.33. Historical-photographic album, Sicilian Province. M. T. FALSONE, Giacomo Cusmano, II, pp. 174; 177; 375.

6. GIUGLIANO DI CAMPANIA (NA). Orphanage

When in April 1880 Mother Rosa visited the community that had been working for two months at the Giugliano hospital, the authorities asked her for three Sisters to run the "Conservatorio for Orphan Girls". The official request was made on 2.5.'80, as the Institute's Prot. 1876-'81, No. 582, shows; she replied clarifying the conditions and arrangements, and once agreement was reached the date was fixed for the three Sisters to arrive in Naples, where they would be met by the hospital Superior, Sr. A. Battistina Bertuzzi, and Canon Giuseppe Marzano. The latter, who had taken the hospital FSA to heart and tried to support them in their charitable work for his "fellow townspeople", on 2 July again urged the Mother to send the Sisters as soon as possible: "...I tell you the need for Sisters in this conservatorio is truly becoming ever more urgent". A scandal had broken out in the town over the report by two doctors (called to the "Conservatorio" to treat two sick orphans) on the appalling hygiene of the place, which they described as "a pigsty rather than a place of education... the little orphans oppressed, neglected, hungry, full of vermin, without any rule or hygiene".

The three FSA — Sr. A. Peppina Colombini, superior; Sr. A. Clemente Bigatti, teacher; Sr. A. Gaudiosa Bertuzzi, cook and portress — arri-

ved probably on 10 August and were at once caught up in major work on the premises. The Superior wrote to the Mother on 16 August: "the day after our arrival [the Administrators] began cleaning the house with whitewashers, carpenter and smith; it is bedlam; we three Sisters are like soldiers in camp; patience... but the hardest part will be contending with those Sisters in the house and with the finances".

The Sisters she mentions were the former directors of the Conservatorio, known in the town as "oblates", who had stayed in the same premises living in community with the orphans. They would be one of the knots hard to untie, along with another no less hard: the Administration's meanness. Under pressure of the public scandal caused by the doctors' report it had fairly promptly remedied the dilapidated state of the premises, but was not so quick to heal the other wound — the wretched and inhuman condition of the poor orphans — by providing decent clothes and shoes, as the Superior kept insisting; in the end she obtained the cloth needed to make the clothes.

Besides restoring the Conservatorio's good name, the FSA helped its finances by teaching in the fee-paying day school that the Administration proposed for girls of "good family", which began on 8 November 1880 with the first four pupils.

Mother Rosa followed the work, supplying a qualified teacher and guiding her Sisters in the difficult task of raising up the orphans and the educational environment. She did not fail to point out to those responsible (3.2.1885) the need for a fourth Sister and for higher pay for the Sisters. Only the second request was granted, the pay rising from £ 250 to £ 400 a year.

But there was someone on the administrative Committee hostile to the Sisters from outside. Don Gennaro Granito Pignatelli di Belmonte, who did much for the FSA, wrote to M. Rosa on 9.1.1886: "Those rascally Administrators of Giugliano have schemed so much that, caring little for what they had agreed with you, they have given the Superior a shameful order not to provide for the house and to ask each time for whatever the Sisters need". And he added: "With prudence, Mother, bring those wicked Giuglianese to heel; but mind, if you withdraw the Sisters from the Orphanage you must at once withdraw them from the hospital too".

The Mother had already received a notice dated 1 January 1886, registered in Prot. 1881-'86, No. 887, together with the reply dated 6.1.1886: "(The President) says he has entrusted the care of the church to a new oblate, taking it from the FSA. It is said that as a result it has been decided to recall all the Sisters from the Orphanage within fifteen days".

The decision was in fact carried out; the exact day the FSA left is unknown, presumably within the time stated above.

Cf. AFSA, Prot. 1876-'81; 1881-'86. Foundations, Giugliano di Campania - Orphanage. D.3.25; D.4.32; D.5.39. B.4.88.

7. FILOTTRANO (AN). Hospital and Home for the Chronically Ill

The request from the President of the Charity Board of Filottrano, which reached Mother Rosa in January 1880 (cf. Reg. Prot. 1876-'81 Nos. 541, 552), was like many others from small towns: three Sisters for the hospital and the adjoining Home for the Chronically Ill. The "small" number, he explains, was justified "by the very limited finances" available and by "the very few patients, barely 80 a year on average... and the chronic cases, usually no more than ten". The formalities completed (ibid., Nos. 555, 570, 593, 678, 606), the three Sisters appointed reached Filottrano on 2 September 1880: Sr. A. Eufrosina Pizzoni, superior, Sr. A. Raffaela Ceruti, nurse, and Sr. A. Guindalina Campora, cook. They were received "respectfully by all... with great esteem and trust", the Superior wrote to the Mother on the day of arrival, marvelling at everything: "I cannot tell you much yet... only that it is truly a splendid place, both for the people we deal with and for cleanliness — for everything, in a word". She repeated this view in later letters.

Although the hospital was ready and in order, there were no patients; they came a few days later.

The "Home for the Chronically Ill", however, was not ready and would not open for some years. Sr. A. Raffaela, skilled at pulling teeth, soon proved her ability to people who gladly came to her, saving themselves not only expense but the trouble of going to Jesi or Osimo.

The work was demanding and highly responsible. Reporting to the Mother after a few months' running-in, the Superior wro-

te: "You will not believe it, but we are surrounded by patients and are busy night and day, without time to feel tiredness or sleep. It is a curious thing: once patients come they never want to leave; even when recovered they look for a thousand new ailments so as to be kept in. We laugh, because everyone, especially [those on] the Board, says: 'There must be a spell on the hospital; before, no one wanted to go there; they would rather die of starvation than go to hospital...'". And she added that, with Saint Anne's help, they had always been able to have the last rites given to the few dying patients.

When the "Home for the Chronically Ill" opened in April 1882 the Mother asked the Charity Board to take on a fourth Sister; this was granted reluctantly, and at half the others' salary, because of the body's "financial state", which required management in line with actual income. She went on defending her overworked daughters before the Administration. Later a fifth Sister was taken on, again at half salary. In 1894 she also had an "economical stove" installed to lighten the Sisters' work.

In 1893 the President of the same Charity Board wished to entrust the Orphanage to the FSA. M. Rosa sent the three Sisters requested, who devoted themselves to the human and Christian formation of the more than twenty girls. This work, dear to the Mother Foundress, continued until 1928.

The FSA's presence in the Hospital and Home lasted almost a century (1880-1975), rich in charity and in Christian and religious witness.

Cf. AFSA, Reg. Prot. 1876-'81. Foundations, Filottrano. D.3.23; D.4.30).

8. CROTONE. "Regina Margherita" Nursery School

The FSA had been in Crotone since 1879 in the orphanage and elementary school and in the hospital (cf. Letters 5, pp. 690 and 691), and it was decided to entrust them also with the Nursery School, which had been running for several years. On 12.12.1879 the President of the Charity Board, Baron Luigi Berlingeri, asked the Mother Foundress for Sisters to replace the present lay Director as soon as pos-

sible, since lodgings also had to be found for the Sisters.

Negotiations went on for several months (cf. Prot. 1876-1881, Nos. 531, 537, 564, 575, 579, 617, 672, 674) until the Sisters arrived on 2 September 1880, the date telegraphed by the Mother. The four Sisters — Sr. A. Nestore Tagliabue, superior, Flavia Sanguinetti, teacher, Arnolfa Gianoli and Filotea Garbi — were lodged at the Orphanage while their own house was still to be found. The Superior and Sr. A. Flavia told the Mother about the journey, their impressions of that unknown world and the events of those days: a visit to the Bishop, talks with Baron Berlingeri, provisional community life. School began on 11 September. A hundred children were present in the single large room that served for everything — lessons, games, meals, rest — from 8 in the morning to 5.30 p.m. The Sisters arrived punctually every day to receive them, after their devotions and breakfast, and returned in the evening after preparing everything for the next day. One Sister made soup for the children in a small, ill-equipped room beside the nursery. The Sisters' lunch was sent by the Superior of the orphanage. So it went on until 21 October, when they moved to a house next to the monastery of St Clare.

The Superior kept the Mother informed about how the work was being organised and received advice, directions and encouragement (L 235). They went on with courage and a spirit of sacrifice, adapting and overcoming difficulties while waiting for the new Nursery School building to be started. Unfortunately the Sisters' health suffered, especially Sr. A. Flavia's, who was confined to bed with fever. The Mother was alarmed: "I want you to keep a close watch on the sick Sister, Sr. A. Flavia; a certain thought came to me", she wrote on 14.2.1881 (cf. L 307).

Very hard months followed for the Superior, the only one unharmed by infection in the unhealthy house where they lived. The doctor called to treat the Sisters said plainly that they must leave that infected place, which had been occupied for years by a woman who died of consumption. The Commission had to find other lodgings for the Sisters. At the end of the school year the Mother had the Sisters, who were slow to recover, leave for treatment, together with the Superior. Only Sr. A. Filotea, now fully recovered, remained.

The FSA who succeeded the first Sisters devoted themselves with the same love and spirit of sacrifice to the children's education until the community was withdrawn on 30 April 1968.

AFSA Prot. 1876-'81; D.3.25; D.4.32.

9. CAROTTO (PIANO DI SORRENTO). Poorhouse - Elementary school

The Archpriest of the Parish of St Michael the Archangel, Francesco Castellano, a zealous and charitable pastor, had turned his own house into a "Poorhouse" to shelter the poorest and most helpless of the parish — the elderly, orphan girls, widows — those who lacked everything, even a roof over their heads at night. To organise this work of charity he decided to turn to Sisters; having met the FSA in Naples he approached the local superior, Sr. A. Speranza Volpini, invited her to visit the "house" and took her advice to write to the Superior General. He did so on 17.4.1880 and received the comforting reply that three Sisters would be sent. The necessary arrangements made, the Sisters' arrival in Naples was fixed for September; the Superior Sr. A. Speranza would accompany them.

Sr. A. Guglielma Merli, the superior, Sr. A. Ignazia Lucchese and Sr. A. Gandolfa Battaglia were instead met by the parish priest's sister on 12 September 1880 and reached the town at 6 p.m., welcomed festively by the people with cheers, flowers and sugared almonds, honoured with a speech for the occasion and solemnly blessed in church during the Eucharistic service.

The next day the Superior gave the Mother her first impressions, as well as news of the journey, and kept her informed of daily events: young women asking to be accepted into religious life, the people, their life entrusted to providence, and the prospects of a work carried on precariously and simply. In reality the poorhouse operated only at night, as a dormitory. The inmates spent their days wandering about, each fending for food and necessities. The Sisters in turn went round collecting alms, and so came to know people and be known.

Their first, dutiful visit had been to the Bishop, who received them very kindly. The people loved them and gave them what they had: "a few coppers and fruit". "While there are figs," the Superior wrote to the Mother on 21.10.'80, "all is well, but now those too are finished. Enough, it will be as God wills; the fact is there is not a single £, either as allowance or salary", for the good parish priest had written to Mother Rosa that he had £ 800 available, but then explained to the Superior that the money was for building the house. On the other

hand, people, seeing that the Sisters "did nothing", kept asking them to take up the education of their daughters. The parish priest suggested opening a needlework school and teaching in the school; through his efforts with the Mayor a suitable solution was found, a Sister teacher being accepted as "municipal schoolmistress". Mother Rosa for her part decided to replace the Sisters with others trained for the new task. She replaced Sr. A. Guglielma Merli (L 239) with Sr. A. Primitiva Boresi as superior and teacher, and added another Sister for the municipal school, who arrived at the end of February 1881 and began with 45 pupils. Examinations were held in early September. But, as could be expected, the results revealed a generally poor preparation, owing to the limited lesson time and the teacher's incompetence. She naturally asked to be moved, and there was no time to replace her with another Sister, as the town council had engaged a laywoman.

Opening a private school was not advisable. To the parish priest who proposed it the Mother replied that she had no qualified teacher available for the moment. They were back where they started. The superior Speranza Volpini, sent there by the Mother, summed it up neatly: "... here we are, doing nothing at all". By the Mother's decision the teaching Sisters had to leave, and on 15.11.'81 the parish priest himself told the Mother of "the misfortune", regretting it and hoping for their return.

Within the year — the exact date is unknown — the others too left Carotto.

Cf. AFSA, Prot. 1876-'81: Nos. 584, 614, 717, 725, 769, 791, 803, 1430. Prot. 1881-'86: Nos. 2, 18, 50, 56. Foundations, Carotto-Piano di Sorrento. Sisters' correspondence: D.3.25; D.4.32.

10. BASSANO DEL GRAPPA (VI). Home nursing. Education of girls

The earliest document concerning the foundation of the Bassano house is a letter from Fr Francesco Chemin (19 July 1880) to Mother Rosa. He had met two alms-collecting Daughters of Saint Anne in Bassano, told them of his charitable project and been encouraged by them to approach the Mother General; they had supported his request by writing at the foot of his letter to Mother

Rosa a telling phrase: "dear Mother, we hope this fine house succeeds".

From the outset Don Francesco was in a great hurry. He spoke of a "most urgent matter", asked for a "prompt" reply, came in person to the Mother House and began work adapting the old monastery of St Catherine, bought to receive "girls in danger and fallen girls". At the agreed time he went to Piacenza to collect the Sisters: Sr. A. Domenica Marchesini (superior) and three others, Pietosa Pennati, Guglielmina Ittile and Gottarda Pompini. He put them up in his own house on the evening of their arrival, 13 September 1880, and took them to their house the next day.

The Superior wrote frequent, detailed reports to the Mother (78 letters from September 1880 to August 1881), which to some extent make up, as a historical source, for the Mother's letters to her, which have not survived. They give interesting details of the daily life of the new work; of the home nursing begun soon after their arrival, requested and appreciated by families, which needed two or three Sisters; and of relations with Don Francesco Chemin and his family, with the clergy and with the people.

Don Francesco was a leading figure. He presented himself as founder, protector and director and tried to exercise those roles to the full: he claimed the right to countersign and post the superior's letters to the Mother, to live in the Institute, and to visit the sick in their homes while the Sisters were nursing them. The Superior responded by explaining firmly what did and did not fall within his role. She could not stop him coming to the Institute every day, as he had to supervise the building work, though he had given that task to his father; but she warned him that it was improper when he stayed on into the evening without reason.

But another matter worried the superior Domenica: Don Francesco's financial muddles. He had bought the old Convent of St Catherine, true, but she understood he had not paid for it. Yet by a regular deed of 16 October 1880 he had given the building and some land in the municipality of Marostica to the Daughters of Saint Anne in the form of a sale for £ ten thousand (as M. Rosa attests in the Statement cited below). In other letters the Superior notes: "He has spent a great deal of money and is sunk in debt; it is true his family is rich, but his father is still alive".

The work came into being gradually. Home nursing continued, and in December '80, the building work finished, the first three girls were taken in. Many others were put forward by parish priests, but it was thought better to wait for financially safer times. On the 14th of that month the opening of the little church attached to the house, dedicated to Saints Joachim and Anne, was celebrated solemnly with the people taking part. The Sisters also helped the work financially by collecting alms and received offerings, though small. Don Francesco was in trouble and did not know how to get out of debt; even his father "absolutely wants to be repaid the heavy expenses incurred on his account". He wrote to the Mother (L 1.12.'81) inviting her to Bassano: only she could help him. The Superior too urged her to come and untangle "such a knotted skein" (L 17.1.'81), or at least to send for Don Francesco.

He went to see M. Rosa in Rome in February 1881 with a priest friend (cf. L 300), pleading his cause and describing what he had done and his plans. Among them was the founding of the Sons of St Joachim to stand alongside the Daughters of Saint Anne; he was ready, as were his friend and other confrères.

He returned home comforted by the Mother's esteem and her encouragement to go on, gradually paying his creditors from the resources he claimed to have.

Meanwhile rumours and criticism had arisen and were circulating in Bassano and the Diocese about Don Francesco, his work and his relations with the Sisters, so the Bishop intervened and took suitable measures: he forbade him any ministry to the Daughters of Saint Anne and forbade them to collect alms.

Mother Rosa was in Bassano from 16 to 20 May. She assessed the situation, was received by the Bishop and briefed on the facts and circumstances, heard his directions and set out the measures she intended to take and the course to follow. She fully agreed with the ban on Don Francesco's ministry to the Daughters of Saint Anne, and it was decided he could only say daily Mass there. She would move the present superior for prudential reasons and entrust the financial question to her lawyer.

In early September the new Superior, Sr. A. Genoveffa Molinari, arrived in Bassano with difficult tasks: to manage the change in relations with Don Francesco, backed by his family, who shared in the financial problems (L 42,6; 427; 431), and to defend the full au-

tonomy of the FSA Institute, both administratively and in the specific functions corresponding to the house's purposes. The thirteen letters of M. Rosa to Superior Molinari published in this volume are a guiding thread to understanding the thorny affair at its most critical moments: the seizure demanded by creditors over unpaid goods bought by Don Francesco, and the return to the Chemins of furniture and objects they claimed as theirs (L 141). The Mother makes her closeness felt: "Courage like a giant, for it is truly needed at this time!... Keep your spirits up... for I am always with you, sharing in everything" (L 444).

The lawyer Alberto Galli of Piacenza went there, studied the situation, reported to the Mother and, on her instructions, entrusted the protection of the Institute's interests to the lawyer Chiminelli of Bassano.

By the end of 1881 the matter had been clarified, and the Mother informed the competent Church authorities of everything (L 506).

The dispute with Biagio Chemin and his son Don Francesco was settled by a compromise. The Daughters of Saint Anne returned the furniture and other objects to the Chemins and kept everything they had bought back with their own money. By public deed of 10 September 1882 they ceded to Biagio Chemin all the land in the municipality of Marostica and bought the Bassano house with its adjoining land for £ twelve thousand, payable within three years to Biagio Chemin, with 5% interest, the land purchased being mortgaged as security.

All this was punctually carried out, and on 18 July 1885, having paid all they owed, the FSA came into free and full possession of the Bassano property.

Don Francesco Chemin seemed to have accepted this outcome, however reluctantly. Yet in 1890 he again pressed his Bishop and the S. Congregation of B. and R. to assert his rights, accusing the Daughters of Saint Anne of having "distorted the purpose" of his donation, "since through their incompetence and lack of care" ten years after the foundation the number of girls sheltered "had dwindled" from 33 to only 10. He therefore asked, through that Congregation, that "the institute he founded be handed over to other Sisters more suitable and fit than the Daughters of Saint Anne" (L 6 October 1890 to the S. Congr. of B. and R.).

On learning of this new accusation, Mother Rosa sent Sr. A. Camilla Valentini to Bassano as visi-tor; she also called

on the Bishop of Vicenza, heard the complaints and accusations Don Francesco had made to him, and presented the real situation. The house was well established; the sixteen girls were cared for and well treated, and the first elementary classes were held in the house for them. The townspeople in general esteemed the Sisters both for their nursing and for the girls' education.

The dispute was settled in the Daughters of Saint Anne's favour by Mgr Beniamino Cavicchioni in a full report dated 20.4.'91, on which we have also drawn for the above information.

In the following years the Institute grew considerably as an educational centre, with Nursery and Elementary Schools, a needlework school, parish and catechetical activities and an aspi-rants' house. It now houses the elderly Sisters.

Cf. AFSA Foundations, Bassano. For the Superiors' and Sisters' correspondence of 1880 and '81: D.3.21; D.3.27. For the Cavicchioni report and other documents of the S. Congregation of B. and R.: C.3.162/VaRc.

11. CASALNUOVO MONTEROTARO (FG). Municipal Elementary School

The correspondence about sending the FSA to the municipality of Casalnuovo Monterotaro took place over five months (30 May-31 October 1880) between the Mayor, Carlo Agnusdei, and the Foundress Rosa Gattorno, and is documented in the Protocol kept by Mother Rosa, with her own entries of incoming and outgoing letters. The Mayor's letters survive in AFSA, but the Mother's are lost. From this documentation we learn about the request for Sisters and the purpose and terms of their teaching. On the Mayor's proposal the town council had resolved to entrust the direction and teaching of the Girls' Elementary School to two FSA Sisters, one for the upper and one for the lower classes. A third, lay teacher, already engaged for six years, would continue until her contract expired.

The Mother pointed out that she could not send only two Sisters and proposed a third. At the Mayor's express suggestion it was agreed that the latter, being in charge of "domes-

tic chores", could not be on the staff; the council would, however, raise the salary of the senior Sister teacher. The Mayor assured her that the townspeople would certainly reward the Sisters with gifts of "the produce of every season, not excluding dairy products, cured meats, chickens, meat", etc. The three Sisters' outward journey was paid and a suitably furnished house provided.

The three Sisters — Sr. A. Adelina Gambaro and Sr. A. Eufemia Ruggeri, for the upper (3rd class) and lower (1st and 2nd) classes respectively, and Remigia Moreni — arrived on 3 November 1880 (Prot. No. 768) and promptly began teaching, earning the townspeople's esteem and admiration, as the Sisters' and the Mayor's letters show. Several young women, including a niece of the Mayor, asked to join the FSA. In time the Sisters had difficulties with unsuitable lodgings, which the council remedied, and with the provincial school authorities over frequent changes of teachers. In informing the Mother of these problems, which affected the pupils' progress, the good Mayor reaffirmed his esteem for the Sisters, "loved and respected by all for their excellent moral qualities", praised the new teacher, who had given "such proof of learning in letters and needlework as to astonish the public", and begged her not to move her like the others (L June 1886). But it was precisely this "excellent teacher" who became the target of the envy of "a troublemaker" and slanderer "holding a school post". The Mother called the Sister to talk with her and on 8 October 1888 asked the Mayor to let her leave the school temporarily; he agreed, asking that she be sent back to her post.

Other influential people intervened in the Sister's defence, but the Mother neither sent her back nor replaced her, and recalled the others.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-'81 Nos. 602, 615, 679, 686, 758, 768. Foundations, Casalnuovo Monterotaro. For the Sisters' correspondence: D.3.25.

12. BREGNANO (CO). Nursery and Elementary School

The Bregnano (Como) nursery school having been made a charitable body, its Committee had appointed

as President the provost Don Carlo Barbieri, charging him with arranging with the Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne for the teaching to be entrusted to two suitably qualified Sisters. After a verbal agreement with the Mother, surely in Piacenza, letters were exchanged (cf. Prot. 1876-'81 nos. 695; 702; 721; 746) and the date of arrival fixed. Mother Rosa duly informed the Bishop of Como (ibid. no. 786). On 6 November 1880 there arrived at Bre-gnano Sr. A. Uberta Chelucci, superior; Sr. A. Deodata Bacchi, teacher of the mixed lower elementary school (1st and 2nd classes); Sr. A. Stanislaa Vignoli, nursery teacher; and a fourth, Sr. A. Ortensia, for the kitchen. Pupils were many: the initial 130 in the nursery soon rose to 160, with 80 in the elementary school. A second Sister was soon needed for the nursery. The full-time school took up most of the day, while Sundays were almost entirely devoted to catechising the good parishioners, who were always respectful and understanding towards the Sisters. The authorities too were good, but "they also watch closely", the Superior wrote to Mother Rosa. The elementary teacher was appointed by competitive examination as a municipal employee. At the end of the 1884-'85 school year, the Mother having withdrawn Sr. A. Deodata Bacchi and the proper documents for her replacement not having been supplied, the council appointed a lay teacher. The Sisters were left with the nursery. But a few years later, chiefly because of the new mayor's hostility towards the Sisters, whose number and pay he wanted to reduce to three, the Mother decided to withdraw the little community at the end of the 1894-'95 school year, in September. Cf. Prot. 1876-'81. Mother Rosa L 436.

13. PALERMO. Pignatelli Institute: orphanage

On 25 September 1880 Canon Ignazio Zuccaro wrote to Mother Rosa on behalf of Archbishop Celesia asking for three Sisters to run the Pignatelli Institute, founded in Palermo in 1842 at the wish of Signora Marianna Monteleone, Princess Pigna-telli-Boviano, "for which purpose she had left all her property, entrusting the direction and administration of the work absolutely to the Archbishop of Palermo pro tempore". Later, however, the Government claimed that right, and only in 1880 did Archbishop Celesia manage to enforce

the testatrix's will and reclaim his rights. The change of administration called for a radical change of educational approach, so Sisters were sought, specifically the FSA. Three were needed, as Superior, bursar and school director, from the following 1 January; the small community could grow fairly soon. The Mother agreed, looked for suitable people for so important and demanding a service and had them ready by the set date. She was able to tell the Archbishop, who pressed her again, that the Sisters had left on 27.12.'80 and would be there on 1 January 1881. On 2 January Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi sent the Mother her first report. Besides Sr. A. Olga Torelli and Sr. A. Giuditta Bianchi, who had come with her, the small community would include Sr. A. Ancilla Briccoli, taken from the Nurses' Community at the request of its Superior, Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi. The handover took place the next day. With the new direction and administration the Sisters began to settle in, introducing changes with tact and patience to avoid friction and resentment among the lay staff, who were used to different methods. Within two years the Sisters numbered 8 and the girls 64. Mother Rosa followed the work through letters, above all to the Superior (cf. L 264, 266, 286, 293, 301, 312, 321, 323, 325, 346, 359, 371, 407, 412, 429, 438, 443, 493), to whom she could also give directions and advice in person when they met in Naples and Piacenza. She also wrote to the Archbishop to clarify problems, and remained close to the other Sisters who wrote to her.

By a document addressed to the Deputy Superintendent of the Pignatelli Institute, Archbishop Celesia, in agreement with Mother Rosa Gattorno, sought to give "a sure and definitive arrangement to the care the good Daughters of Saint Anne" had undertaken, fixing their number at 8 Sisters with the following duties: Superior-director, two qualified teachers for the Elementary School, a needlework teacher, a bursar, a nurse, a cook and a portress; and setting out relations with the Archbishop and the general lines of organisation and management. The girls received an integral human and Christian formation, with a basic education in the elementary school and training in needlework, especially embroidery.

The work prospered, helped by the endowment income. In 1909, through Cardinal Lualdi's efforts, it was mo-

ved from its original premises in Via Giovanni di Giovanni near the Politeama to the larger and finer Villa Florio at San Lorenzo ai Colli.

The FSA carried on the educational work with love and dedication, handing down over the years the educational principles instilled by Mother Rosa. Various reasons, including changes at the Pignatel-li and above all the shortage of Sisters, forced the community's withdrawal on 30.6.1986.

Cf. AFSA, Protocol 1866-'81. Foundations - Palermo "Pigna-telli". For Fiocchi's letters to Mother Rosa F.5.41. For Archbishop Celesia's correspondence G.1.2. For the Sisters' correspondence D.4.33; D.5.40; D.6.47.

14. ROME. Incunabolo (Nursing room)

"The incunabolo, or nursing room for babies", had been set up at the "Tobacco Factory" in Piazza Mastai 11, Trastevere, to help working mothers during the period of breastfeeding: each day, during working hours, they could leave their babies in safe hands, go to them to feed them when needed, and collect them at the end of the working day.

This socially very useful service to families, especially working mothers, was proposed to Mother Rosa in February 1881, when she was in Rome; she accepted wholeheartedly and took a personal part in setting up the work, beginning with its regulations. Her draft (cf. AFSA, Foundations Rome, Incunabolo) shows her competence and organisational skill. She told her daughter Carlotta and son-in-law of this commitment: "I have good news for you: listen, I have accepted a crèche. Ah! what a lovely place, fitted out with every elegance! ... and it means a great deal of work for me; I must do everything... I have had all the layettes made in the big shop in Via del Corso, the finest ... everything is already in order" (L 324, 4-5). And a few days later: "on Monday the 14th (March) the crèche opens" (L 326). She chose Sr. A. Berta Belliti as Superior, with Paola and Clotilde; a few months later she added Sr. A. Ausiliatrice Bessi and Sr. A. Serafina.

When she left Rome the work was well under way. On 21 March the Superior Belliti wrote to her: "the babies' house, by God's grace, is going wonderfully... Today the Commendatore came with the other

gentlemen, and they praised its cleanliness. Every day ladies and gentlemen come to see the place, and all congratulate us warmly. But we are so busy we have not a moment to ourselves". The Sisters had one great difficulty: having to go early every morning from their house in Vicolo Marga-na to Trastevere, it was not easy to attend Mass daily. The Mother had already asked the Director to prepare a suitably furnished room for the Sisters, which at last they could use on 13 June. "Tomorrow night we shall sleep at the factory for the first time", the Superior told Mother Rosa (L 12 June). It was a great relief, as the Sisters were exhausted by evening. The work was unceasing. Every morning, as soon as the babies arrived, the Sisters dressed them in the Incunabolo's clothes, each child having its own registration number and a personal compartment in a special wardrobe; in the evening, before handing them back to their mothers, they reversed the process, urging the mothers to take the same care and keep them as clean. During the day the babies' needs were attended to with the utmost care, the doctor being called promptly for extra visits as well as routine ones. The children's personal hygiene and that of the cradles and rooms was kept with the greatest care. The number of little ones (30 a day on average) speaks for itself of the Sisters' overwork and of the responsibility inherent in this delicate motherly task.

In 1886, because the number of women workers, and hence of babies, had fallen, the "Administration of the Royal Tobacco Concession" reduced the Sisters to three, and in 1891 the Ministry of Finance ordered the nursing room closed. The decision was notified to the Superior General Mother Rosa Gattorno on 16 July 1891. The few babies were entrusted to some of the workers. The FSA's presence ended at the close of that year.

Cf. AFSA Foundations Rome Incunabolo. For the Sisters' correspondence to M. Rosa: D.4.31; D.5.37; D.5.45; D.6.52.

15. RUFFANO (LE). Hospital - Home nursing - Nursery School

The first intermediary between the local authorities and Mother Rosa regarding the FSA at Ruffano was Fr Agostino Donadio, to whom the Bishop of Ugento, Mgr Gennaro M. Maselli, his con-

frère, had turned to deliver the petition "to the proper person". The Bishop wrote on 21.3.'81 that Ruffano had decided, "on the most favourable and flattering terms, to establish a house there for the FSA, and they would like three Sisters as soon as possible, two for the hospital and a duly qualified teacher to instruct the girls", adding: "I am sure that if these Sisters are well received I shall have the comfort of establishing them in other towns of my Diocese".

Mother Rosa accepted the proposal and, in response to the request of the President of the Charity Board, Sebastiano Pasanisi (cf. L Fr Agostino to M. Rosa: 3.4.'81), prepared four Sisters but sent only two: Sr. A. Virginia Gaggi, Superior, and Sr. A. Massimina Carola (L 360). For the moment they would help "in setting up the hospital and practise the charity of home visits to the poor". The two Sisters arrived on 12 April, welcomed with great deference at Brindisi by two members of the Board and escorted to Ruffano, where not only the authorities came out to greet them but the people too turned out, cheering and saluting them with marks of esteem and veneration.
