They busied themselves among these people, visiting the sick from house to house, meeting distressing poverty, and grieving at the immense needs and their own helplessness and poverty. Sr. A. Virginia unburdened herself to the Mother: "the Sister of Charity who was here some time ago gave so much in alms; what can we do? We come empty-handed". And she described at length all that was expected of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Visiting and nursing the sick at home and in hospital; running the nursery school and any other girls' institution that might be set up; distributing medicines to the poor designated by the Board; preparing food for the sick poor at the Board's expense. In short, the town's humanitarian and charitable work was in their hands.

On the following 1 May President Pasanisi thanked M. Rosa for the Sisters' presence and work and asked her to "send the other three to complete the number needed for the work assigned to them". That same month Sr. A. Irene Carmeli arrived for the Nursery School, with Sr. A. Ermelinda Bianchi and Sr. A. Celestina. On 10 August a 25-year agreement was signed. Everything was thus set in order, both in the hospital and nursing sector and in the School. The Mother judged it wise to replace the Superior Virginia and the director Sr. A. Irene with people better suited to the place. From

October the Superior Geronima Amiel and Sr. A. Nestore Tagliabue were there.

In 1882 the Administration asked the Mother for a sixth Sister qualified in pharmacy, a task of great responsibility and work. Nothing came of it because of difficulties on both sides, above all on the charity's part: a large administrative deficit came to light. The consequences were the Committee's resignation and nine months of administration by a commissioner, the treasurer's prosecution and trial, and the hospital's closure. The two nursing Sisters did not abandon the patients sent home; they visited and treated them daily, receiving nothing from the Administration. Eventually it was decided to withdraw them.

Mother Rosa agreed to leave three Sisters in the nursery school. But in view of the new Administration's proposal to make the agreement with the Sisters directly responsible rather than with the Superior General, she decided to withdraw them, giving notice on 13 March 1885.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-'81, Nos. 885, 889, 107, 1460. Foundations - Ruffano. For Fr Agostino Donadio's correspondence A.2.96/1-2; 33-34. For the Sisters' correspondence D.4.32; D.6.54.

16. PRATO. Home nursing - Orphanage

The first approaches for this work date from August 1880 and appear in three letters to Mother Rosa from Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, Superior of the Pistoia house. On 11 August she wrote: "I have had good news about the Prato house; I hope it will soon be settled; preparations are already under way" (cf. L 179); on 15.8: "on Wednesday Fra Pellegrino will come to talk to me about Prato"; and three days later: "it seems they want us for the School and as nurses. For the house they have plans outside the Gate".

Nothing more is known of the Superior Crocifissa's mediation, for she left Pistoia, going first to Rome and in 1881 to Palermo as Superior of the Pignatelli Orphanage.

Those interested in the project then approached the Superior General directly. In Protocol 1876-'81, No. 833 we read these notes in M. Rosa's hand: "Requested for home nursing by people who undertake to pay a sum for their keep".

And on the facing page: "8.1.1881. The Superior of Pistoia is being sent to arrange matters; she will put everything in order and then (the Sisters) will stay".

The protocol omits the names of the "people who undertake to pay for their keep", but they gain prominence and credit in the letters of the Sisters who, accompanied by the Superior of Pistoia, Sr. A. Geronima Mazza, reached Prato on 9 May 1881 — above all the Canon and Prior of Sant'Agostino, Flaviano Magni, and Fra Pellegrino. In her report to Mother Rosa (undated L) Sr. A. Geronima gives, besides the date of arrival, the main news: the house intended for them was still occupied by tenants, so Canon Magni had put them up. She had called on the Vicar General, who received them kindly, took an interest in the Institute and advised them on starting their service in Prato. A benefactor or two were already in view. They would soon begin home nursing, and later alms-collecting, once the people of Prato had come to know and appreciate their charitable work. More news comes from the letters of the Superior Sr. A. della Natività Rapillo. The first Sisters — Sr. A. Fruttuosa Balestro, Sr. A. Zenaide Sabini, Sr. A. Andrea Cammarata — were joined at the end of June by Sr. A. degli Angeli D'Alessandro, Sr. A. Franca Falò and Sr. A. Leonide Minotti.

In August Sr. A. Bianca Bronchi succeeded the first Superior. These Sisters' letters tell the story of the early period, woven of daily acts of genuine heroism. They worked hard, nursing the sick night and day at great sacrifice, relying on providence through "alms-collecting" for their own keep, and busied themselves preparing the rented house with the bare necessities. They moved in on 1 November, and at the end of that month had the joy of welcoming Mother Rosa to the "new House", which seemed to them fine and spacious (cf. L Bronchi to M. Rosa: 24.8.'81) but which in reality, according to the historian F. Franchi, "was a small flat on the top floor of the Palazzo Cecconi in Via Luigi Muzzi, made of attics turned into rooms; the best room was the little chapel, which looked like the crib at Bethlehem". The "Annine" made themselves known, esteemed and loved by the people of Prato, who supported their work from the start and helped it grow into one of the city's most renowned educational institutions.

In 1884 Mother Rosa entrusted the community to Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, who set out to develop and extend in Prato the work

of the FSA. First another house had to be found and bought with the help of some generous benefactor. Canon Magni sent her to Canon Leopoldo Franchi (later Vicar General of the Diocese and then Bishop of Livorno), who not only gave of his own but found generous benefactors — Fr Benedetto Dominici, Signor Enrico Bresci and others — so that with their help Mother Rosa was able to buy and adapt a small house with a large garden at Via Pallacorda 195, opened on 3 August 1886 (L La Barbera to M. Rosa n.d.). Some orphan girls were taken in there, at first two, then three more.

The turning point came with another figure: Canon Silvio Ceccatelli. He was not only a distinguished benefactor but the father who took the work to heart and launched it. On 6 December 1892 the Superior Sr. A. dell'Angelo Tosca wrote to Mother Rosa: "the (girls') confessor has made it his business to win our poor Institute a little renown. He has now issued a little circular about taking in day girls to prepare them for First Communion". The Mother replied that she would send a Sister and involve the Superior Amante, who was glad and encouraged the Canon's plan to found an institution for abandoned orphan girls.

Thus, with the full consent of Mother Rosa and the Church authorities, the Little Educatorio of Saint Anne in Prato was born, to which Canon Ceccatelli "devoted all the energy of his life, assisted by the FSA, who, more than tireless, devoted and patient collaborators, were the base and foundation on which he could build the Work", of which he is regarded as founder and father. (Cf. F. Franchi op. cit. in note).

After Canon Ceccatelli's death (2 February 1945) the Little Educatorio, under the FSA's guidance and improving year by year, remained a centre loved by the people and blessed by providence until 1976, when, owing to the well-known shortage of religious personnel, the Sisters were withdrawn and the premises given to the Diocese for "the apostolic and social works of the Local Church".

Cf. AFSA. Foundations - Prato. Prot. 1876-'81, No. 833. For the Sisters' correspondence with Mother Rosa F.5.41; D.4.31; D.5.37; D.5.45; D.6.52; D.7.58; E.1.3; E.1.7; E.2.11; E.3.15; E.3.18; E.3.21.

For historical information: S. FRANCO FRANCHI - Quarantanni di vita del Piccolo Educatorio di S. Anna in Prato (1891-1931) - Bechi Prato 1831.

17. LEGNANO (MI). College for Deaf-Mute and Blind Girls

In 1867 negotiations had begun between Fr Aquilino Marelli, parish priest of Cerro Maggiore, and Mother Rosa about a Patronage for deaf-mute girls he wished to found. Having at his disposal "the house, a church, people willing to become nuns, land and money", he had, on the advice of Don Ghislandi, director of the "Royal Institute for the Deaf and Dumb" in Milan, approached Mother Rosa, who was willing to take on the direction of the Work. But obstacles arose and the plan was dropped. (Cf. Letters 1, L 49 and 63).

In 1881 Marelli came forward again. He had founded at Legnano the "S. Angelo" College, where he housed needy girls: thirty deaf-mutes, seven blind girls, some boarders including two invalids, two servants (as farmhands), three as orphans and seven servants, entrusted to some Sisters. As the correspondence shows, having gone to Piacenza in person and then by letter, he undertook to carry out the Mother's suggestions: to dismiss the surplus staff and to separate the FSA's sphere of work from that of the other community already there. The date for sending six Sisters was fixed: 18.5.1881 (cf. L Marelli to M. Rosa: 12.5.1881).

The Superior Santina Solenghi accompanied them. They were Sr. A. della Concezione, Superior, Sr. A. Colomba, Sr. A. Monaca, Sr. A. Al-cantarina, Sr. A. Teodosia and Sr. A. Del Carmelo. During the week they tried to get things started in an orderly way, but the situation was delicate. Sr. A. Colomba, in charge of the deaf-mutes, sent the Mother a first report on 28 May through the Superior Santina, who would tell her everything. The separation made was inadequate; prudence was needed. The kitchen was shared, with two FSA working in it; another was permanently at the door; one nursed the sick.

In June the Mother, passing through, visited Legnano (L 383) and left Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega there for a time; improvement was hoped for. Mass in the house was not possible, not even on Sundays. The deaf-mutes became attached to the Sisters. One group did embroidery; most worked at "winding", processing silk with Sr. A. Colomba, on commission from a local firm.

The Director, Fr Marelli, lived at Cerro Maggiore. He appeared only occasionally and was slow to hand over the agreed £ 5 a day to the Superior.

His management was in deficit and he tried to put it right as best he could. From August '81 Sr. A. Colomba, besides the deaf-mutes, was also Superior. In frequent letters she complained of the privations they endured. The baker would not give the daily bread on credit; one morning she resorted to polenta to feed girls and Sisters.

On 18 September (cf. L 436,2) Mother Rosa went there and managed to clarify and settle the administrative problem (cf. L Sr. A. Colomba to M. R. 24.9.'81). The Superior took over the management: she was to collect the proceeds of the silk-winding and of the embroidery done by the deaf-mutes.

When the post of teacher at the municipal nursery school fell vacant, the Provost of Legnano, Don Domenico Gianni, asked Mother Rosa Gattorno to have one of her Sisters apply; documents were submitted but the result was negative.

Despite the difficulties, and though the problem of the Director Don Marelli's debts remained not fully resolved, 1881 ended for the community in hope and growing trust in Providence, which at Christmas was generous beyond all expectation: firewood, wine, panettoni, etc. — the winter supplies the Superior had not known how to obtain.

A further way of settling the disputes over the College's administration was the formation of a Committee to provide, legally as well, for the preservation of the Institute for Deaf-Mutes. The Daughters of Saint Anne had won esteem and renown in the town.

Then some decisive events occurred. In 1884 the Cantoni cotton mill set up an orphanage for working girls aged 12 to 14 in part of the S. Angelo College building, leased to it by the Director Marelli. This additional work was separated off by suitable structures. At the request of those concerned, Mother Rosa provided two Sisters solely for the girls' instruction.

But Duke Cantoni had another plan: to buy the whole complex, which suited Marelli, who saw at last a chance to pay off his debts. Mother Rosa, informed of the plan, prepared for possible solutions. On 30 April 1886 the Director Marelli told her the sale was under way, and later announced the transfer of the Institute from Legnano to Cerro Maggiore. The Archbishop of Milan, informed in person by the local Su-

perior and by the Provost of Legnano, advised withdrawing the Sisters (cf. L of the Provost to M. Rosa: 30.10.'86). On 1 November Mother Rosa told the Director Marelli that if "within 20 days conditions had not improved" (L of Marelli 3.11.'86) they would leave.

In 1890 the Cantoni Orphanage was also closed and the three Sisters were freed.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-'81 Nos. 886, 891. Foundations - Legnano. Sisters' correspondence to M. Rosa D.4.28; D.4.35.

18. CROTONE. Foundling Home

As mentioned above under No. 8, the FSA were engaged in Crotone in educational, welfare and health work. When a Provincial Foundling Home was to be set up in the city, Councillor Raffaele Lucente was asked to sound out the Superior General of the FSA about the possibility and terms of providing two Sisters for its internal service, one as Director and the other as Supervisor, also in charge of the kitchen. The Protocol 1876-'81 shows an exchange of views in the negotiation (Prot. Nos. 881, 884, 893), concluding that the Administration would take three Sisters at a combined salary of £ 1000 plus board and lodging, etc. Later agreements fixed the Sisters' arrival for 6 August, then postponed it (Prot. Nos. 945, 954, 103). On 11 August the travel money was sent. The day of arrival is unknown, surely between 25 and 30 August. Writing to the Mother on 1 September, the Superior Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni apologised for not writing sooner because of all there was to arrange. With her had come Sr. A. Filippina and Sr. A. Alessandrina. They found only one wet-nurse and one baby. The house had no chapel; she was trying to set a timetable. She was worried because she had been told the Sisters would have to accompany the wet-nurses on walks — a supervisory task, to ensure they kept the rule forbidding them to speak with anyone, husbands included. This did not seem to her suitable or fitting for Sisters; later it was remedied by giving the task to a layperson.

The Sisters' presence was a sound guarantee of order, good running and morality, as is clearly stated in an inspec-

tion report for 1887, an extract of which concerning the Sisters was sent. It reads:

"As to the moral condition of the charitable institute, the name of the Sisters of Saint Anne, to whose direction it is entrusted, is a sound guarantee. These Sisters, all in general and the Superior in particular, attend zealously to order, morality and discipline; they not only surround the infants with motherly care but are an example of virtue and a practical school of morality for the wet-nurses, who, when unhappily they are not wholly free of fault, leave the home, one may say, purified" (certified extract signed by the President F. Albani and the secretary).

Over the years Superiors and Sisters changed without harming the work. In September 1905 the Director asked Mother Benedetta Carrega to replace the Superior as "unsuited to the internal direction" of the Foundling Home. In January 1907 the replacement of the three Sisters was requested for the same reason. The following July the Superior General announced the decision to withdraw the Sisters for reasons concerning the Institute.

Cf. AFSA Foundations - Crotone Foundling Home. Prot. 1876-'81, numbers cited. For the Sisters' correspondence D.4.32; D.5.38; D.6.53; D.7.63.

19. PALERMO. "Ardizzone" Orphanage

The Institute took its name from its Foundress, the Marchioness Maria Teresa Ardizzone, who established it by deed of the notary Marco Antonio Averna dated 1 May 1818 to take in orphan "maidens" from Messina, Rometta and Palermo, aged 7 to 10, until they were 18, and give them a suitable education, training them in needlework and housework. They were to wear a uniform like that of the "mistresses and officers" and to work in turn in the kitchen, laundry and any other task in the house assigned by the staff, who held the posts of Superior, vicar, portress, sacristan, storekeeper, cook and four teachers.

The statute for the Orphanage's administration was approved by Royal Decree on 13 August 1876. This information, given in a study of the houses for our Congregation's centenary (cf. references in note), besides being a reliable historical

source, explains how the work developed and the situation the FSA faced when in 1881 they took over from the lay educators, who after a long period in charge found themselves replaced by outsiders — and not even Sicilians. They stayed on in the orphanage, it is true, but in a subordinate position. Hence the understandable and justifiable "hostility" towards the newcomers, though they knew their presence had been wanted by the Vicar General, Mgr Giovanni Cirino, president of the Orphanage.

On his behalf Mgr Ignazio Zuccaro, secretary to the Archbishop of Palermo, Michelangelo Celesia, had written to Mother Rosa Gattorno on 2 August 1881 asking for three Sisters — a Superior to manage the finances, a lower-grade teacher and a cook — each to be paid £ 50 a month. He explained that some employees would remain in the house: the portress, a secretary and a girl for small tasks.

Mother Rosa accepted but asked that a fourth Sister be taken on; the request was refused for lack of funds (L Zuccaro to M. Rosa: 18.8.'81), so they began by sending three Sisters, entrusting the new work to Sr. A. Crocifissa Fiocchi, Superior of the Pignatelli Institute, who became the link between the two parties and kept in touch with the Mother, telling her of each step and asking her advice and clarification. After visiting the "little convent of Saint Anne or Santa Annuzza — as the people called it after the nearby church dedicated to Saint Anne — lovely, with a garden and amenities", accompanied by the Vicar Cirino (L 15.9.'81), she brought the Sisters there the following Sunday, 20 September 1881: Sr. A. Leonarda Innocenti, Superior; Sr. A. Amedea Bellacima, cook; and Sr. A. Clemente Bigatti, transferred from the "Pignatelli" (L 443). Sr. A. Leonarda and Clemente too wrote to the Mother (cf. their letters of 22, 25 and 28 September '81), each giving her own picture of the situation.

"The welcome from the former occupants, 'the two nuns of the house', and the servants is rather cold". There were only 12 girls, who "have not a scrap of discipline and lack clothes". "There is strict enclosure even for the girls; they go out only three times a year".

"The Superior Crocifissa is a mother to us; she comes to see us almost every day," wrote Sr. A. Clemente, "and after eight days the Archbishop too came to visit us". She ended optimistically: "with Saint Anne's help, all will turn out for the best".

On 29 October the teacher Sr. A. Irene Carmeli arrived and the School opened (L Fiocchi to M. Rosa: 31.10.'81). But the Sister found it hard to settle; the Mother managed to persuade her (L 459; 460; 462; 476). She also wrote often to the Superior Crocifissa, helping her carry out necessary decisions, including the change of Superior: Sr. A. Clemente in place of Sr. A. Leonarda, who was moved to the Nurses' House (L 461; 467; 473).

But difficulties persisted, caused by interference from the old staff and resulting misunderstandings with some members of the Administration, so that withdrawal of the Sisters loomed. The Mother discussed the problem with Archbishop Celesia during his visit to Rome. He advised her not to move: everything would be sorted out. Reassured, she wrote to the Superior Fiocchi, advising her and urging her to stay with the Sisters for a few days (L 486; 489; 491). The difficulties were gradually smoothed out, while Mother Rosa made herself present by letter and by prayer (L 493; 499). After some months the Vicar had a priest examine the girls on their schoolwork, and all showed good preparation and a marked change; so too at the final examinations in June 1882. In the face of the girls' progress and the positive changes in the atmosphere, prejudices fell away, and little by little during 1882 a climate of harmony and serenity took hold: "As regards the house," the Superior wrote to M. Rosa on 9.12.'82, "I give endless thanks to the Lord and to Mother Saint Anne that such peace is kept between us and the people we live with".

In 1886 the Superior Sr. A. Clemente Bigatti was succeeded by Sr. A. Irene Carmeli, who was also director and remained at the Institute until her death in 1920.

Over the years the Ardizzone became well known as an educational centre, also because of its attached Elementary and Nursery Schools, attended by girls from the most distinguished families of the city's historic centre; and when in 1935 costly repairs to the building became urgent, offerings to cover the expense poured in, the Superior General of the FSA contributing by waiving the Sisters' annual salaries (£ 6,700) from 1 January 1936 for as long as needed. The FSA served without pay for three years, as a letter of the Superior Apollinare Andreoli dated 31.3.39 shows.

After the war the Elementary and Nursery School was expanded with new buildings in the garden of the orpha-

nage. Teaching was given by the Sisters, who also ran the administration until 1971, when, owing to the shortage of personnel, the Superior General had to withdraw them and management passed to the Administrative Council of the Ardizzone charity. On 28 August 1973 the other Sisters working in the orphanage were also withdrawn.

Cf. AFSA Foundations - Palermo Ardizzone Inst. On Mgr Ignazio Zuccaro G.1.5. Sisters' correspondence D.4.33.2; D.5.40.3; 45.41. The Mother's letters in this volume are cited in the text.

20. ROME. Home nursing

Princess Sofia Odescalchi, advised by Fr Agostino Donadio, asked Mother Rosa's help in founding a "charitable work", namely nursing the sick poor in their homes. On 27 July 1881 she explained that she meant to rent, to house the Sisters, a small house in Vicolo del Piombo belonging to her son, Prince Ladislao Odescalchi. She had "entrusted the new work to the three parish priests of Santi Apostoli, Santa Maria in Via Lata and San Marcello, to organise a monthly offering from their parishioners and see to its collection", thus sparing the Sisters from begging. She herself would direct it, so the Superior was to agree with her so that together they could make the greatest possible savings.

On 22 October she wrote again asking her to appoint a capable Sister as Superior, with a companion, to finish and arrange the premises in Via del Mancino, and urged that they be sent within a few days.

On 26 October '81 Sr. A. Antonietta Gallinari and Sr. A. Flora Bog-gioni went to the Princess to receive instructions about the house. The other four Sisters followed and began home nursing (cf. L Fr Agostino to M. Rosa: 12.11.'81).

In 1882 the community of nursing Sisters moved to the house in Vicolo del Piombo, rented from Prince Ladislao Odescalchi.

The Princess had set up a capital fund whose income would ensure payment of the rent.

The Sisters remained there until 1948.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-'81, Nos. 944, 953. Foundations - Rome House Vicolo del Piombo. Correspondence Fr Agostino Donadio B.5.98; Sisters D.4.31; D.5.37.

21. CASTIGLIONE DI SICILIA. Municipal Elementary School

Negotiations for the FSA's presence in Castiglione date from the last months of 1880.

On 30 September 1880 the Archpriest Vincenzo Sardo informed the Mother Foundress that the town council had resolved to entrust "the education of the town's girls" to the Daughters of Saint Anne. Three qualified Sisters were therefore requested, each to be paid £ 500, plus a furnished house. The Bishop of Acireale, Mgr Gerlando Maria Genuardi, had been informed of everything and had given his approval. The Sisters were wanted by early November.

This could not be done so quickly, first because Mother Rosa Gattorno, though she accepted promptly, had pointed out the need for a fourth Sister, and also because of the notoriously slow official procedures for approving teaching staff.

The councillor responsible for education, the engineer Giuseppe Lamonica, a convinced supporter of the project, took its realisation to heart, corresponding with the Mother about the staff and their qualifications, their lodgings and the premises.

On 17 July '81 he wrote about the latter that, with the Holy See's prior nihil obstat, he had obtained part of the Benedictine Monastery for the school and the Sisters' lodging. The work of restoration and furnishing now had to be carried out.

The Sisters the Mother assigned to the new work reached Aci S. Antonio on 30 August and, before going on, called on the Bishop at Aci Reale to receive his blessing. He welcomed them "with great kindness" (cf. L 2.9.'81 of Sr. A. della Carità Gariboldi to M. Rosa) and then telegraphed Castiglione for the Sisters to be fetched. On 1 September the councillor Lamonica came to them but could not take them with him: the house was not ready and needed more than a month to complete the essentials. In fact two months

passed (cf. L 28.10.'81 of Sr. A. Tommasina Viterbo, Superior of the Aci S. Antonio house, to M. Rosa).

At last, to everyone's relief, the 4 Sisters set out on 3 November 1881: Sr. A. Della Carità Gariboldi, Superior and teacher; Sr. A. Clelia Giacoboni and Sr. A. Cirilla Costa, teachers; and Sr. A. Zoe Mar-chiorri.

The next day the Superior wrote the Mother a long letter with interesting details about the places, their welcome, the people, the furnishings and the prospects for expanding the FSA's work in the near future. Two postulants were already waiting.

A few days later the school opened with 70 girls. Councillor Lamonica wanted two of his daughters educated by the FSA, and the Archpriest a niece; they stayed as day boarders.

The Mother, consulted by the Superior and informed of how the work was being set up, advised, approved and encouraged. The engineer Lamonica too was in constant correspondence with her, both about the Elementary School and about the other works entrusted to the FSA: the Regina Margherita Orphanage, where the three Sisters he requested arrived on 21 September 1885 (cf. L 21.9.'85 eng. Lamonica to M. Rosa), and later the St John of God Hospital, whose negotiations, begun on 18 August 1886, suspended and resumed in 1889, ended with the Sisters' arrival in September of that year.

There is no reliable information on when the FSA stopped teaching in the municipal Elementary School. The engineer Lamonica's letters to M. Rosa give news of its running; in 1903 he also wrote to Mother Carrega asking for a Sister teacher, which seems to be the last mention. Presumably, as elsewhere, lay staff were gradually introduced by competitive examination into teaching in state schools, helped by new regulations.

The FSA provided nursing in the hospital until 1950, when their withdrawal was judged advisable for lack of religious personnel.

They remained at the Regina Margherita orphanage until 1996.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-1881, Nos. 733, 738, 855, 856, 866, 894, 903, 905, 906, 916, 927, 985. Foundations - Castiglione di Sicilia. Sisters' correspondence D.4.33.

22. CONVERSANO (BA). "Regina Margherita" Nursery School

"The Administration of this Nursery School having resolved to entrust the children's education to the motherly care of Sisters of Charity, our excellent Bishop, the Archbishop of Bari and the Archpriest of Rutigliano, whose letter of introduc-tion you will find enclosed, advise me to apply to the good Sisters of Saint Anne".

This preamble to the request for two Sisters for the Nursery School, addressed to M. Rosa by Fr Flavio Laricchiuta on 31 August 1881, is one testimony to the good name the FSA enjoyed in Apulia too among bishops and clergy. The Mother accepted but could not send fewer than three Sisters; she explained why and set out the conditions she usually kept to. The correspondence for further clarification and agreement was, as the AFSA documents show, between the Mother and Fr Flavio Laricchiuta, succeeded in December '81 by the President of the Nursery School Committee, Mgr Nicola Ratti. He wrote her a long letter (19.12.'81), introducing himself as "the Bishop's deputy to care for your daughters". He described in detail the arrival of the three Sisters, whom, as the Committee had decided, he met at Mola di Bari on 6 December 1881 and took by carriage to Conversano; he put them up in his house for four days while some ladies hastened to prepare a fitting welcome in the lodging reserved for them by the Nursery School on the outskirts of the town.

The Superior, Sr. A. Placida Garampazzi, for her part hastened to write to M. Rosa as soon as they arrived, and again on 9 December, praising the kindness of the Bishop and Mgr Ratti and the courtesy of the people of Conversano.

School began on 12 December, run by the Superior and Sr. A. Balbiana Carbonini, while Sr. A. Ottavia Lagostina was in charge of the kitchen.

In 1882 a fourth Sister was granted; a chapel was opened in the Sisters' quarters; the children increased, and as the years went by praiseworthy results were achieved to general satisfaction, President Ratti and his successors not failing to express their pleasure to the Mother.

In 1896, at the end of the school year, the President V. Rutigliano told the Mother that the government Inspector's report had highly praised the Nursery School, rating it "among the first in the Kingdom, especially for results". All this was due to the skill

of the excellent teachers. But precisely for this reason the Mother more than once met strong resistance from the Committee over transfers. This, besides the body's financial difficulties, was one of the reasons for the FSA's withdrawal from the "R. Margherita" Nursery School in 1908.

Cf. AFSA. Prot. Nos. 1250, 1260, 1290, 1370. Foundations - Conversano. For the Sisters' correspondence D.4.32.1,4; D.5.38.

23. RUTIGLIANO (BA). Nursery School - Hospital - Poorhouse

Arrangements for the opening go back to 28 October 1880, in a letter to M. Rosa from the Archpriest Gianvito Chiaia, a member of the local Charity Board, explaining the reason for the invitation and the Board's charitable and welfare project. He wrote: "...having learned from the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Archbishop of Bari of the admirable qualities of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, I write to you and formally invite you to provide, from November of next year 1881, five Daughters of Saint Anne to run the Nursery School and to nurse and administer the Hospital of this Town...".

Having noted the Mother's acceptance and the conditions she set out on the following 4 October, they spelled out the mutual agreements, concluded on 12 November 1880 with an agreement signed by the members of the Charity Board and sent to Piacenza for the Mother's signature.

One clause stated: "the Mother General undertakes to send to Rutigliano, in the second half of October next year, five Daughters of the Institute...".

In the following period the practical arrangements were made. In Prot. 1876-'81 we find M. Rosa's careful record of incoming and outgoing letters concerning the house, its furnishings and whatever else might help the Sisters.

On 25 November the new Bishop of Conversano, Mgr Casimiro Gennari, informed of the Daughters of Saint Anne's coming to Rutigliano and Conversano, wrote to the Mother that they were expected between the 4th and 6th of the following month, adding: "your Daughters are wanted by everyone, for their merit and virtue are well known...". With notice given, the Mother sent them for that date, and on 6 December the five Sisters arri-

ved in Bari. They were met at the station by some members of the Commission and three Sisters of Charity and told that, as their house was not ready, they would have to stay 8-10 days with those Sisters. The Superior informed the Mother by telegram and letter, and she thought it best to visit Ruti-gliano to find out and give more precise information. Cf. L 493.

At last, on 15 December 1881, the Daughters of Saint Anne, accompanied by two Sisters of Charity, reached Rutigliano. Sr. A. Assunta Saccani, Superior, and her companions Clarenza Devoto, Aureliana Butti, Sara Medica and Davidina Rossi were welcomed by the notables and people with the solemnity of great occasions, and in their honour there was a gala dinner attended by the town authorities — the Archpriest, the Mayor, the Charity Board's Commission, etc. — and by the Sisters: the five Daughters of Saint Anne and the two Sisters of Charity, who besides putting them up had also prepared the linen for their house. After a few days settling in, the Nursery School opened on 21 December with about a hundred children. The other planned works were then completed. On 21 January 1882 Archpriest Chiaia congratulated the Mother on the Sisters: "...All of us in the Administration and the whole Town are pleased and happy with these good and excellent Sisters, blessed Daughters of Saint Anne, whom you sent here; the Most Illustrious Monsignor and I in particular are very pleased with the excellent qualities and virtues of these Sisters".

On 19 September 1882 he wrote again on the opening of the Poorhouse and Hospital: "Your blessed daughters have given striking proof of charity, sacrifice, diligent and wise care, self-denial and toil. Praised be holy Mother Saint Anne, who knew how to choose these angels of charity".

The FSA continued their work, five in number (two in the Nursery School, three in the hospital, poorhouse and care of the elderly), for many decades. From 1967 the documents make no mention of the Nursery School. But the five Sisters remained for the hospital and welfare service, and some years later rose to seven to meet the needs of the enlarged and more efficient hospital, until 1975, when the Superior General of the time withdrew them owing to shortage of personnel.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-'81, Nos. 783, 792, 865, 882, 933, 1180, 1260, 1280. Foundations - Rutigliano. For the Sisters' correspondence D.4.32.4; D.5.39.

24. BUSSETO (PR). Hospital

Negotiations between the Mayor of Busseto, as President of the Busseto civil Hospital, and the Superior General of the FSA began on 22.7.1881 and were conducted with good understanding and clarity. Three Sisters were requested "for all the internal service of the hospital", formally engaged from 1 January 1882 on the terms of an agreement signed on 16.8.1881, similar to the one in force between the FSA Congregation and the management of the Borgo S. Donnino Hospital. The Sisters were to be there at least 15 days before "the date of the contract" and arrived punctually on 15 December 1881, accompanied by the Superior of the Borgo S. Donnino Hospital, Sr. A. Camilla Valentini, who stayed for some time to start them off in their demanding task, as an expert. They began by "putting everything in order", trying to keep faith with their promises to the Mother. "I am well and very happy to be here... I want to do all I can and will study everything so that all goes well; the Sisters too are willing; we hope, with Saint Anne's help, to do the Institute credit and be your consolation". So wrote the Superior, Sr. A. Onorabile De Vincenzo, on 20.12.1881, also on behalf of her companions Sr. A. Concezione D'Alessandro and Sr. A. Onorina Astolfi.

They went on with such dedication as to win esteem and admiration, so that two years later, when the town set up an isolation hospital for cholera patients in case the disease spread, the Mayor decided "to entrust its direction and service to the nursing Daughters of Saint Anne", who were doing "so much good in the Civil Hospital too". Mother Rosa kept four ready, but happily the fears were not realised. Over the years further agreements were made: in 1911 the number of Sisters was raised to five; in 1935 a "home" for disabled elderly people was attached to the hospital and two more Sisters were requested.

Sisters succeeded one another, devoting themselves in daily sacrifice to the sick and the old for almost a hundred years. But in 1973, for lack of personnel, the four remaining Sisters had to be withdrawn; three of them, elderly, were moved to rest homes.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-'81 Nos. 942, 952. For the Sisters' correspondence D.3.27; D.4.34.

25. CHIARAVALLE (AN). Incunabolo

The Daughters of Saint Anne had been caring for babies at the Rome Incunabolo since the previous March (cf. above, no. 14), so when the Administration of the Italian Joint-Stock Company for the Royal Tobacco Concession decided to set up another nursing room at the Tobacco Factory in Chia-ravalle, it counted on the Daughters of Saint Anne.

M. Rosa agreed to the request for five Sisters (1 October 1881).

On 18 December 1881 Sr. A. Ausiliatrice Besso, Superior and director of the "Nursing room", arrived with her four companions. That same day the Superior told the Mother of their welcome: "if you had seen how many people were waiting for us! They came to the station with two carriages; the director was there too... such kindness! We found everything in order". The next day they began work. Twenty-two mothers, happy and grateful, entrusted their little ones to them.

Mother Rosa was close to her daughters by letter too, encouraging them. "I understand you want us to be an example to this town," the Superior replied on 22 December to her "dear letter"; "we do all we can, and with Saint Anne's help I hope all will go well. The parish priest has spoken of us to the Bishop and said he is very pleased with us".

This most beneficial work was, however, closed by the Ministry of Finance because of the small number of babies. The Sisters left at the end of June 1896.

Cf. AFSA Foundations Chiaravalle. For the Sisters' correspondence D.4.30; D.4.36.

26. MATERA. Hospital

In Prot. 1876-'81, No. 905, 31 May 1881, Mother Rosa recorded as outgoing the note "to Michele Gattini of the Counts of (illegible): the Rutigliano contract and conditions sent", and in No. 906, 2 June: "The Bishop is asked for permission to enter the Diocese"; and again in No. 206, n.d., she renewed her request to him for consent.

The Archbishop of Acerenza and Matera, Mgr Gesualdo Loschiri-co, replied on 13 July. He had spent two months visiting the towns of the Dio-

cese, which explained the loss of letters addressed to him. From Cav. Gattini he had learned of all that had been done to bring her good Daughters of Saint Anne to his city; the gentleman in question was a model of honesty and courtesy, from a most religious family, and she could be confident her daughters would be well treated and respected. For his part he promised to use his poor influence in whatever way he could.

Meanwhile negotiations with Cav. Gattini continued, the contract was concluded and the departure of four Sisters agreed; the Mother wished to send them with those already assigned to Conversano and Rutigliano (L 487). This proved impossible: they had to wait another month, as the hospital was to be handed over on 1 January, so it was best for them to leave on the following 28 December. That very day they reached Bari, where the Archbishop received them "so kindly". He had them lodged with the Sisters of Charity, and the next day they continued their journey.

Sr. A. Alfreda Paolotti, Superior, and her companions Teodora Barisioni, Reparata Santioli and Eduarda Carboni reached Matera on 29 December 1881.

The welcome, the Superior relates in her L of 30 December, took place in the Cavaliere's palazzo. Waiting for them were the Archpriest and the gentlemen of the Hospital Administration; the Archbishop too, who had come to call on the master of the house, wished to greet the Sisters when he learned they were there. The next day the Superior returned the Archbishop's visit and asked him to appoint a confessor for the community; he assigned an Augustinian. In conversation he spoke of his wish to open an orphanage for orphan girls and those who wandered the streets begging, and to call the Daughters of Saint Anne to run it.

That same day the Sisters visited the hospital. Their first impression dismayed them. "What an impression the disorder and dirt made on me and the Sisters!" the Superior wrote on 31 December, "but I hope that little by little, by God's grace, I can put things in fair order, and the Board members too are very eager to meet our needs". The Commission, talking with the Sisters, wished to hear what the duties should be of the male nurse working with them and of the woman for heavy work, and the doubts about this were cleared up.

On 1 January 1882 they were handed "the linen and everything needed for the hospital. Whatever is lacking will be provided as soon as possible".

The Superior completed her account of the first days with a note of gratitude to Cav. Gattini: "Signor Gattini showed us every possible kindness during the days we stayed in his house, and on New Year's Day too, after the handover, he wanted us to come back to lunch with him".

The archive documents on the hospital's foundation are a rich historical source on the growth and running of the work and on the remarkable contribution of the many Daughters of Saint Anne who have succeeded one another there and who still work there, mindful of the witness of charity and self-denial of the Sisters who went before them.

Cf. AFSA Prot. 1876-'81, Nos. 905, 906, 924, 926, 941, 114, 1400. Foundations - Matera. For the Sisters' correspondence D.4.32; D.5.39.

Translation in progress: for now, the Italian text.

Il biennio 1882-1883 costituisce un momento decisivo per la storia della Congregazione delle Figlie di Sant’Anna e per la sua Fondatrice: ad uno sguardo retrospettivo, infatti, si può notare come esso rappresenti quella linea immaginaria che divide proprio a metà i 34 anni di vita consacrata della Beata Anna Rosa Gattorno a servizio dell’Istituto da lei fondato e della Chiesa tutta. E non è soltanto una considerazione formale, che di per sé offrirebbe lo spunto per una curiosità passeggera, sebbene priva di un riscontro sostanziale: quel breve spazio di mesi corrisponde, a ben vedere, alla fase forse più cruciale del lungo e travagliato iter dell’approvazione delle Regole, un passaggio delicatissimo segnato dalle numerose correzioni (le cosiddette animadversiones) che la Congregazione dei Vescovi e dei Religiosi formula in merito, e a cui la Madre risponde con sincera sottomissione e devota obbedienza (Lettere 62-64), fugando ogni sospetto di insubordinazione; contemporaneamente (siamo tra i mesi di febbraio e marzo dell’ ‘82) il Pontefice accorda all’Istituto che il primo Consiglio Generalizio possa costituirsi tramite il Cardinale Protettore ricorrendo alla votazione per posta, e a breve distanza di tempo viene impressa una accelerazione decisiva ai cantieri della Chiesa e della Casa Generalizia di via Merulana (LL 255 e 269); frattanto la missione boliviana irrobustisce il nucleo iniziale di La Paz e Sucre col nuovo polo di Cochabamba, forte di un flusso costante di Religiose disposte ad affiancarsi alla ’pioniera’ suor Anna Camilla Valentini che già dal 1878 viveva in Sud America in pianta stabile. L’importante decisione sul possibile invio di un primo gruppo di suore in un ospedale in terra di Sicilia, dove già Agrigento (1876) aveva aperto una prima breccia, riceve un sigillo definitivo con il promettente viaggio della Madre nell’Isola – il primo in assoluto – che risale proprio al gennaio dell’ ‘83. Ultima notazione, ma non per questo meno significativa, nel dicembre dell’ ’82 (L 210) la Madre rischia di morire, ma ottiene la guarigione per intercessione di Maria Mater Gratiae et Misericordiae, inaugurando idealmente una nuova e ancor più entusiasmante pagina della storia dell’Istituto.

Accanto agli importanti eventi appena ricordati, si dispongono in sequenza lineare tutta una serie di circostanze rispetto alle quali la presenza di Madre Rosa si è connotata costantemente nei termini della vigilanza materna, della premura accorata, della ferma giustizia, di una carità senza confini ove l’adesione al dettato della Croce ha fatto da collante ad ogni decisione e da garanzia di sicura coerenza tra pensiero, azione e grazia.

La pubblicazione di questo ulteriore segmento della sua nutritissima corrispondenza aggiunge, dunque, un tassello importante nell’ampia parabola già tracciata con i precedenti sei volumi, e fornisce ulteriori elementi per una valutazione sempre più precisa del governo di una Congregazione destinata proprio in quel periodo ad estendersi a macchia d’olio – “essendo che l’Istituto va ognor più dilatandosi”, dice la Madre nella L 399 –, anche fuori dall’Europa (alla imminente “partenza delle Americane” si allude nella L 437), e a rinforzare le proprie posizioni là dove già in precedenza erano stati gettati dei semi piccoli, eppure assai fecondi.

Da un punto di vista formale le lettere mantengono inalterata quella stessa struttura già riscontrata in precedenza, sebbene le sempre più intense sollecitazioni esterne che andavano a gravare su un fisico sempre più indebolito da “lunghi e penosi” viaggi (L 160), dalle cefalee intermittenti e dalle febbri (cfr. L 163) incida in modo sostanziale sull’ampiezza di testi ormai sempre più brevi e vergati in alcuni casi pure sotto dettatura (“sono costretta ricorrere ad altra penna”, dice in apertura della L 312), dove frasi poco precise dal punto di vista grammaticale o lasciate in sospeso dimostrano una mancata revisione del testo, resa impossibile dall’incalzare degli impegni.

Ad ogni modo, mano a mano che si procede nella lettura delle lettere qui edite si verifica qualcosa di sorprendente: sembra, infatti, che i profili dei personaggi coinvolti assumano via via contorni sempre più netti; che le figure, cioè, si trasformino – da abbozzi appena tratteggiati – in ritratti a tutto tondo, diventando più familiari, riconoscibili, quasi che se ne possano prevedere a un certo punto i moti dell’animo, le attitudini, le richieste, persino le risposte. E ciò avviene anche per la Madre, qui come non mai forte nel suo vigore di eroica Fondatrice. La sua lucidità e la sua lungimiranza sono elementi costanti che sottotraccia ne connotano l’operato: frequenti, per esempio, sono le esortazioni rivolte alle suore perché assumano una mitezza che non scada mai nei toni del servilismo; o, ancora, gli sforzi profusi nel ridimensionare i comportamenti negativi di qualche suora improvvida, suggerendone con discrezione l’allontanamento. Madre Rosa dimostra ogni volta una spiccata capacità di discernimento, e sa valutare in quali circostanze più liberamente delegare, per evitare che il suo governo sia interpretato nei termini dell’autoritarietà assoluta; le esortazioni a mantenersi lungo il solco di una vita sobria, dove ogni sovrappiù può offrire al Nemico terreno fertile per attecchirvi la sua zizzania, convivono col rammarico per inevitabili imprudenze registrate qua e là, alleviato dal convincimento che sia “dolce patire per un eterno godere”!

L’attenzione per delle faccende che forse al lettore contemporaneo apparirebbero di secondaria importanza, la risposta a dei pareri tutto sommato non decisivi per la vita di una comunità religiosa, ci dicono di una fiducia incondizionata delle suore per la Fondatrice, alla quale si cerca di garantire sempre una obbedienza fedele e amorevole. E la Madre, per nulla infastidita da richieste incessanti che potrebbero disorientare o procurare pesanti affanni, non perde mai di vista il fine ultimo della propria missione, richiamandosi sempre al Crocifisso come Sommo bene Suo e, implicitamente, delle sue Figlie. Impressiona la sicurezza, ma anche lo sforzo con cui seleziona le persone (“dopo di essermi aperta il cervello”, afferma coloritamente nella L 22): siano esse delle Superiore sostitutive, o delle Sorelle da inviare in case che muovono i primi passi o ancora degli ulteriori rinforzi per infoltire nuclei preesistenti. Nel caso specifico della costituzione del nucleo fondante di una nuova casa seleziona le suore una ad una, perché ne conosce il profilo psico-fisico e attitudinale, e arriva addirittura a prefigurare possibili sostituzioni equivalenti.

Madre Rosa è capace, allora, di predisporre, pianificare, organizzare, formulare persino assetti alternativi in caso di rinuncia o di inadeguatezza. Rimprovera e biasima con parole coloritissime – “brutte creature, serve indegne del Signore che fanno da manutengole” (L 83) – ma sempre per il bene dell’Istituto, senza quel risentimento e quell’asprezza che attirerebbero solo disaffezione e inimicizia. La Madre è amatissima, al punto da diventare interlocutrice anche per questioni delicatissime di ordine spirituale: una lettera brevissima e in apparenza irrilevante (L 78) dà la misura del grado di confidenza che le Figlie rivolgono alla Madre, la quale suggerisce in questo particolare frangente l’approccio migliore alla confessione. Una premura multiforme, la sua, capace di rispondere alle aspettative più diverse; un’attenzione che naturalmente non risparmia la figlia Carlotta e il genero Gaspare, come pure i beneamati nipotini a cui riserva le sue cure speciali (doni, promesse, tenerezze; preghiere fervide e accorate specie per la guarigione della cagionevole Nonni), per non dire del figlio Alessandro che tanta pena le procura con i suoi comportamenti elusivi e menzogneri.

Madre Rosa si rivela prudente nelle valutazioni, ai benefattori non fa mai mancare segni concreti di sincera gratitudine, accompagnando epistole cordialissime con promesse di presenti ed espressioni concrete della propria riconoscenza: così è nei confronti del professore Francesco Alberti, il destinatario più presente nella corrispondenza vagliata, cui si rivolge con cadenza settimanale perché prepari le Suore al conseguimento del titolo abilitante alla docenza negli Asili e nelle Scuole Elementari. Un benefattore generoso, che intercede presso il Ministero della Pubblica Istruzione per istituire delle Sessioni straordinarie di esami ad hoc per le Suore ed ottiene persino uno sconto del 50% sui biglietti ferroviari della rete nazionale (L 392). Quella con l’Alberti è comunque una corrispondenza altalenante, in cui convivono espressioni di entusiasmo per il buon esito di una sessione speciale, assieme agli sfoghi avviliti e mortificati per l’inadeguatezza della preparazione di alcune Suore che la stessa Madre definisce ” inabili ” ma per le quali chiede indulgenza, conoscendone l’impegno e la bontà: l’Alberti si amareggia, minaccia persino l’abbandono della causa (cfr. L 353), ma la Madre insiste perché la sostenga nel continuo braccio di ferro con le amministrazioni – “sono proprio seccanti i comuni” (L 201) – che non mancavano di fare ostruzionismo, ingolfando il lavoro nelle scuole che attendevano l’impiego delle Suore abilitate.

Forte di una memoria prodigiosa, la Fondatrice ricorda alle destinatarie l’ammontare di crediti e debiti, le faccende da concludere, gli attori da coinvolgere. Impressiona la sua avvedutezza nella gestione delle finanze, rivelandosi economa impareggiabile: arriva in un caso a richiedere un estratto-conto – “mi mandi i conti in regola che io, ripassati e bene osservati che li avrò, non tarderò a pagarlo” (L 211) – poiché nulla le sfugge, e perché nulla possa dirsi affidato al caso. I mal di testa la assediano senza lasciarle requie nemmeno di notte, ma questo non la trattiene nel farsi attenta ai bisogni che le giungono da sempre più parti, dove gli attori si moltiplicano e le relazioni si fanno sempre più complesse e aggrovigliate. Talvolta è costretta a degli estenuanti equilibrismi, per disattenzioni riconducibili ad altri e a cui ella deve riparare con umiltà profonda (L 166), allora escogita dei correttivi utili a sanare delle fratture non volute.

Col suo stile inconfondibile la Madre comunica sempre una confidenza affettuosa – “troppo mi state in mente!” (L 16) e si fa prossimità dolce e incoraggiante: accenti incalzanti i suoi, che quasi anticipano i piani di Dio: “Io non so capire come sia che non si possono aprire altre case in questa parte. Basta, lasciamo tutto nelle mani di Gesù. Esso tutto per noi farà.” (L 16). Presagendo quale grande parte avrebbero avuto sr. A. Celsa Speranza e sr. A. Benedetta Carrega negli anni a venire, garantisce loro l’invio costante di missive più dettagliate e dai toni ancor più intimi e confidenziali. Emblematico poi, il passaggio di una lettera a sr. Anna Irene Carmeli (L 92) dove le conferma la possibilità di pronunciare i voti perpetui con l’esclamazione “Per una eternità mia!” Madre Rosa esprime in parole l’amore di viscere materne che lei nutre per le Suore. Quel possesso per l’eternità non è, allora, traduzione verbale di un appannaggio esclusivo, quanto invece un riconoscimento e di appartenenza anche nell’Aldilà – dove, cioè, la totale oblazione della Madre per le sue Figlie potrà dirsi definitivamente compiuta e soddisfatta. E non stupisce se, con tutt’altra qualità di tono e a pochi giorni di distanza, riprende prima una Figlia, facendole sentire tutto il proprio affetto confidenziale con parole tenerissime e giocose – “Sono dolente di sentire che sei stata poco bene. Brava, perché non me lo hai scritto? Cattivella!” (L 104), mentre a sr. A. Carrega racconta spassosi aneddoti («Oh! che ridere oggi non ho fatto appresso a Sr. A. Giu... ci si dice un pero e capisce un persico…» - L 111), dimostrando un’umanità autentica e calorosa che per tante Figlie è stata garanzia di incoraggiamento e di conforto. Ed è un’affezione credibile quella che la Madre nutre per le Figlie, perché da una parte non ricusa di esternare le proprie afflizioni, le paure anche ingiustificate che possono tormentarla (cfr. L 129), e dall’altra pretende reciprocità (“non mi lasciate senza vostre lettere!”, L 341). Ancora, le espressioni colloquiali che intercalano il discorso aggiungendo una nota del tutto confidenziale (“senti, mi raccomando, mi capisci?, per carità!, basta, dai…vedi? mi sono spiegata? ma che vuoi.. che ti pare?”); sono la manifestazione sincera di una voce prossima, che vuole tradursi in vicinanza concreta, seppur preclusa in più occasioni dalle incombenze di governo. A supplire, eventualmente, ci sono gli insegnamenti impartiti – condensati in forma ufficiale con la Lettera Circolare del 9-10 marzo 1883 (L 273) – condivisi poi ‘a cascata’ alle tante Figlie delle varie Case, e sempre coerenti con la Regola, che rimane vero “scudo e trionfo” (L 409) di ogni vocazione duratura. Questa reciprocità, questo appartenersi a vicenda in un rapporto di autentica figliolanza si manifesta sempre con linguaggio familiare – “figliuola, i tuoi Superiori chi sono? Non sono forse il padre e la madre? E perché dunque ricorri ad altri e non al Padre o a me quando hai bisogno di qualche cosa?” (L 347) – cui si aggiunge il desiderio cocente di sobbarcarsi ogni dolore – “Vorrei potere assorbire tutte le pene delle figlie di S. Anna ed esse tutte piene di felicità!” (L 288) – e facilitare così ad ognuna la corsa verso la salvezza eterna, avendo come costante riferimento la Madre Sant’Anna – “Che devi temere se tieni una Madre così potente, che sfida l’inferno intero?” (427) e i divini decreti che Madre e Figlie sono chiamate ad ‘adorare’ (LL 416 e 419).

La notizia della morte dei due nipoti l’ha colpita duramente. La esorta a guardare con fede e amore Gesù crocifisso e la Madre sua. Si affidi a Lei e si faccia coraggio. Curi la salute e sia forte.

Cara Francesca,

1 Che ferita!2 Ma Gesù nostro tutto per noi fu flagellato; Maria, Madre diletta, ne ebbe da riceverlo in grembo e pure teneva il suo sguardo fisso all’Eterno Padre “fiat voluntas tua!” ne andava esclamando! È pure regina dei martiri! Maria!

2 Figliola, tieni stretta l’Addolorata, nella tua afflizione guarda Maria! Ti consolerà. Maria rasciugherà le tue lacrime e (ti) metterà pace al tuo cuore riempiendolo dell’amore di Gesù! Esso solo ci può consolare.

3 E beati loro che già ne possederanno la bella corona immortale, là tutto è festa, pensa che un dì dovevano essere in pericolo di ciò che è di più prezioso in terra ed in cielo; il tutto, l’anima.3

4 Dunque figliola, coraggio, non lasciarti prendere dalla malinconia. Per carità, cerca di svagarti; non dico che tu vada dalla Mamà, no! Perché anche Federico lo zio dice che non va bene con la tua poca salute.

5 Già venendo eletta ci vedremo presto.4 Ti raccomando la tua salute, non ti accorare, pensa che di questi sei sicura di vederli nella beata patria del Paradiso.5 Non lasciarti prendere dalla debolezza. Infine coraggio. Vorrei ancora trattenermi teco ma sono stanca assai e ti assicuro che questa notizia mi ha ferito. Mio Dio! che pene, tutte per amor vostro!

Addio, scrivimi: ti lascio nel Cuore di Gesù e sono tua,

aff. M. R.
